# Pax Silica and the Philippines — independent assessment (full text)

> Complete text of the assessment as published at https://pax-silica.aiailabs.net/,
> generated from the rendered page. The live page adds the interactive exhibits,
> the claim-checker filters, current news coverage, and the version and
> verification dates. Publisher: Agile Intelligence (https://www.agileintelligence.ph).

## The six findings

### 01 — the instrument does not describe the project
The published BCDA offer proposes a bilateral coordination office and states that the property "shall be used exclusively" for five coordination functions. It contains no reference to semiconductor packaging, data centres, mineral processing, or private locators. The public prospectus has no published legal basis.
Key figure: 0 (references to industry in the operative instrument)

### 02 — the headline figures do not reconcile
Pairing US$40–70bn with 130,000–190,000 direct jobs is unreconciled and jointly implausible: constructible on paper, but the one illustrative mix this report constructed needs more back-end employment in this one site than the whole national industry supports today, and no published mix reconciles them. The claimed PHP 68–75bn of annual withholding tax, which BCDA has confirmed is payroll withholding, implies average pay of PHP 2.13m at an assumed 20% effective rate and 160,000 jobs, 2.4 times what a Philippine semiconductor engineer earns. The named anchor is expected to generate "thousands."
Key figure: 2.37× (exports vs. 2025 export book · period unspecified, nominal scale only)

### 03 — water and power are unsolved, not solved
Harvesting 90 MLD from rainfall needs a catchment of 1,460–3,129 hectares, or 90% to 193% of the site. 3 GW is 19.2% of the DOE’s 15,600 MW projection for 2026 Luzon peak demand and 20.6% of the 14,534 MW actually recorded by mid-2026, on a grid that ran a 373 MW deficit under red alert in May 2026. The DFC is funding an LNG feasibility study, not a solar one.
Key figure: 15,000 ha (land a solar-powered 3 GW would need. the site is 1,619.)

### 04 — the counterparty relationship is asymmetric
On 24 July 2026 a US 12.5% forced-labour tariff on Philippine goods took effect. Narrower than the headline: semiconductors and other Section 232 articles are exempt, and it replaced an expiring 10% measure, so the net increment is about +2.5 points. The direction is what matters. The Philippines is being asked to grant land, water, power and rent forgone in exchange for a non-binding declaration and feasibility studies.
Key figure: +2.5pp (net tariff increment, four months before the philippines is asked to sign)

### 05 — sampled sentiment fell sharply by july, most negatively on the unanswered questions
In the provider-stated 10% sample, relabelled on one scheme from January to late July by the same software that labels the daily collection, net sentiment toward the project among relevant sampled mentions ran between +25 and +51 in the early months, fell to +5.3 in June, and fell to −35.6 in July. Sampled mentions on the economics ran both ways. Sampled mentions matched to water, land and governance were strongly negative under the export’s vendor labels and keyword categories, at net −44, −50 and −54. These are machine-labelled sampled mentions, not a measure of the Philippine public’s views. The running exhibit above tracks the conversation daily.
Key figure: −35.6 (net sentiment in july among sampled mentions, the month of most claims and fewest documents)

### 06 — the strategic case is genuine, and some criticism is wrong
Comparative non-entanglement with Chinese capital is a real and time-limited asset. BPO at 7.4% of GDP faces AI displacement. And some of the most widely circulated environmental critiques do not survive scrutiny: silicon rather than nickel is the semiconductor input, and the light-pollution claim, while a legitimate and mitigable screening item, is substantially overstated as popularly framed.
Key figure: 7.4% (of gdp: the bpo exposure that makes an alternative engine urgent)

## The full assessment

### 01. Prefatory note on timing and currency
Why the timing matters, and the conventions used throughout.

This report’s first edition was completed one day before President Marcos’ fifth State of the Nation Address of 27 July 2026, which Malacañang trailed as containing an "earth-shaking" announcement. As of v2.8 the SONA is incorporated from the Official Gazette transcript and no longer sits outside the evidence base; project facts move forward as developments are verified.

Four developments in the fortnight before cutoff are material enough to drive specific conclusions. The anchor tenant has been named: Foxconn, the same company whose Wisconsin project delivered a fraction of its announced investment, which converts the "announced versus delivered" comparison from an analogy into a direct precedent involving the same counterparty. Official job claims have escalated to five mutually inconsistent figures issued by four arms of government within a fortnight. The United States imposed a forced-labour tariff on Philippine exports on 24 July 2026. And a signed ACWA Power lease provides a hard land-per-megawatt benchmark that permits a rigorous test of the renewable-power claim, a test the claim fails by a wide margin.

All conversions use PHP 61.85 per US$1, from US$1 = PHP 61.847, the peso’s record-low close of 24 July 2026. Where a source gives a peso figure it is reported as given and converted; where a source gives dollars, the peso equivalent is calculated.

This is a living document. Project facts are verified to 17 September 2026 and move forward as material developments are verified. Comparator, legal and technical sources were verified through 27 July 2026 and move only when those are re-verified.

[sources drawn on: T3-21 · T1-05]

### 02. Backgrounder: Pax Silica and the world that produced it
The transaction cannot be judged without the system it belongs to.

For roughly three decades the semiconductor supply chain was organised by cost alone: designed in the United States, printed on Dutch machines, fabricated in Taiwan and Korea, assembled and tested in the Philippines and Malaysia, from minerals refined wherever it was cheapest, increasingly China. Geopolitical disruption was a tail risk, not a design constraint. What ended that arrangement was a decade-long exchange of blows: China’s 2010 rare-earth halt against Japan; the Huawei entity-listing; the October 2022 export controls; the CHIPS Act and the European Chips Act; gallium and germanium licensing in 2023 escalating to an outright ban in 2024; the H20 ban and China’s seven-rare-earth restriction in 2025; and extraterritorial rare-earth controls in late 2025, suspended for a year under a trade truce. Both superpowers have now repeatedly demonstrated willingness to weaponise their chokepoints, and every economy in the chain is being asked to buy an insurance policy.

The alliance’s logic is complementarity, not symmetry. ASML holds a true 100% monopoly on EUV lithography; Arm sits under more than 99% of smartphones; SK Hynix and Samsung hold roughly 80% of high-bandwidth memory; TSMC dominates the frontier. Against them China holds 98–99% of primary low-purity gallium, about 91% of refined rare earths and about 94% of magnets. Southeast Asia holds assembly, test and packaging, which is the Philippine seat at the table, with electronics at more than 54% of national exports.

The least visible chokepoint is capital. Design costs run from about US$42.8m at 28nm to US$89.8m at 16nm, US$249m at 7nm, US$449m at 5nm, US$581m at 3nm and roughly US$725m at 2nm. Geology is not enough and neither is labour: a country holding minerals or assembly capacity but standing outside the allied capital and licensing umbrella is structurally marginalised. That is the coercive underside of the positive-sum language, and it is why membership grew from 7 to 25 signatories in eight months.

Compute has also turned electricity into a membership qualification. Qatar signed on 12 January 2026 and the UAE on 14 January; the physical anchor is the 5 GW UAE–US AI campus in Abu Dhabi, the largest AI infrastructure project outside the United States. This is the same energy-for-compute logic that makes the 3 GW question at New Clark City the decisive Philippine feasibility issue. In this system, electricity is the entry ticket.

The architecture was built in a single week of February 2026. Project Vault, announced 2 February, is EXIM’s largest financing in 92 years, up to US$10bn plus about US$2bn of private capital, creating a U.S. Strategic Critical Minerals Reserve across all 60 USGS critical minerals. FORGE, announced 4 February, supersedes the Minerals Security Partnership with a preferential bloc built on coordinated price floors enforced through adjustable tariffs. Pax Silica is the third stage: the demand anchor. The 4 February Ministerial that launched FORGE is the same event at which the Philippines signed its Critical Minerals MOU.

This sharpens rather than changes the assessment. Standing wholly outside carries documented exclusion risks that fall hardest on an economy whose exports are 54.3% electronics. But the system is explicitly tiered, explicitly US-arbitered and explicitly designed around revocable access. Membership is therefore not the prize; position within the membership is the prize, and position is determined by exactly the instruments this report finds undetermined: the lease terms, the processing obligations, the technology-transfer covenants, the governing law.

[sources drawn on: T1-01 · T1-06 · T2-01 · T1-41]

### 03. Executive summary
Nothing is legally binding, financed, contracted or permitted at the project level.

The Philippines has joined a United States-led political initiative and has publicly offered approximately 1,618.74 hectares of BCDA-owned land in New Clark City, Capas, Tarlac, to host its first Economic Security Zone. As at the latest verification, nothing about the project is legally binding, financed, contracted, or permitted at the project level.

What exists is a non-binding declaration signed on 16 April 2026 by a Department of Trade and Industry undersecretary; a four-page proposal letter from the Bases Conversion and Development Authority dated 9 April 2026; a named but uncommitted anchor tenant; roughly thirty unnamed letters of interest; and a contemplated framework or master agreement that Philippine officials hope BCDA and an unidentified US counterpart will sign in November 2026, potentially during an ASEAN Summit that President Trump is expected to attend.

The published BCDA offer does not describe the project the government is marketing. The headline economic figures are unreconciled: no published activity mix reconciles the capital and job figures, and the tax figure is not reconciled with the employment figure at current wage benchmarks. The two binding physical constraints, water and power, have not been shown to be soluble on the published parameters. The counterparty relationship is markedly less favourable than the framing suggests. And, in fairness, the strategic case is genuine and some of the criticism is wrong.

The recommendation is neither endorsement nor rejection. It is that the Philippines should not sign an instrument creating substantive rights before the required conditions are met; a strictly non-binding framework is acceptable only with every express safeguard of the two-branch rule. Legal leverage continues until substantive rights are created; political lock-in may increase around the November target.

[sources drawn on: T1-02 · T1-03 · T1-05 · T1-14 · T1-42]

### 04. Key judgments
Sixteen judgments on a five-point confidence scale. Structured analytical judgments, not calibrated probabilities.

The Pax Silica Declaration is a non-binding political declaration, not a treaty and not a legally enforceable executive agreement. It imposes no obligation and confers no entitlement. Every benefit invoked in Manila (investment, technology transfer, upskilling, market access) is unsecured by the instrument actually signed. Confidence: high.

No investor has made a binding, disclosed commitment. The published BCDA proposal describes a bilateral government coordination facility with an exclusive-use clause covering the entire 4,000 acres, not a multi-tenant industrial park. The US$40–70bn investment figure and the 130,000–190,000 jobs figure are unreconciled and jointly implausible. A mixed-use configuration delivering both is arithmetically constructible, but the one illustrative configuration this report constructed would require more back-end employment inside this one site than the entire national industry supports today, and no published activity mix reconciles the two. The impossibility claim is withdrawn; the disclosure demand stands. Official employment claims are inflating without new evidence.

On-site rainwater harvesting alone has not been demonstrated as sufficient at the stated 90 MLD demand. A 3 GW load cannot be served by solar on the site or elsewhere in New Clark City, though whether an off-site renewables-plus-firming configuration could work is unmodelled by anyone, and marked as such. The immunity and jurisdiction question is unresolved, not closed. BCDA’s claim that no indigenous community is affected rests on the absence of a titled ancestral domain, not the absence of a claim.

The "resource plunder" critique is substantially overstated as applied to semiconductor demand, though a narrower minerals concern remains legitimate. The claim that the project is purely commercial with no defence dimension is not sustainable as stated, though an on-site defence function is expressly not established: what is established is a strategic-security linkage and a gap between framing and statements by Philippine officials. The distributional profile below is a structured risk hypothesis pending the undisclosed instruments, not a finding. And the project is pre-decisional rather than underway: fourteen of sixteen implementation gates are open, a status BCDA itself confirmed in a formal FOI denial of 12 May 2026. How much leverage the Philippines loses on signature depends on what the November instrument actually creates, which is why the decision rule below turns on the rights a text confers rather than on its label.

[sources drawn on: T1-05 · T1-03 · T3-03 · T3-06]

### 05. What is known, claimed, disputed and still unknown
The claim-verification matrix: fifty-four claims adjudicated.

Known and verified: the Declaration text and its 25 signatories; that the Philippines signed on 16 April 2026 through a DTI undersecretary; the complete text of the BCDA letter including the two-year grace period, the undefined Year-3 rate and term, the reversion clause, the exclusive-use clause and the statutory miscitation; the US fact sheet’s "joint governance" language; the US-Philippines Critical Minerals MOU of 4 February 2026; the ACWA Power 500-hectare solar lease; and the USTR tariff of 24 July 2026.

Claimed but unverified: every economic figure in circulation, investment, jobs, taxes, exports, GDP share, originates with the Philippine government and rests on studies that have not been published.

Disputed: immunity and jurisdiction; the number of affected farmers and indigenous households; whether the project is renewably powered; whether it has a defence dimension; the scale of the minerals linkage.

Unknown: the framework text; the identity of all interested firms; the identity of the "US-based company" described by BCDA as project proponent; the Year-3 rent; the lease term; the metes and bounds; the water balance; the grid interconnection plan; the incentive package and its fiscal cost; the domestic value-added assumption; and whether Senate concurrence will be sought.

[sources drawn on: T1-01 · T1-02 · T1-03 · T1-05 · T1-14 · T1-15 · T4-01 · T1-41]

### 06. Definitions and boundaries of the project
Public debate conflates at least eight distinct things.

Separating them is the single most important analytical step in this file. The Pax Silica initiative is a US State Department programme with no legal personality. The Declaration is a short non-binding political text with 25 signatories. Philippine accession was a political act with no domestic legal effect. The proposed Economic Security Zone is a proposal only. The Pax Silica Coordination Office is what the BCDA letter actually proposes. The Luzon Economic Corridor is a separate initiative, announced April 2024 as a US–Japan–Philippines corridor and expanded on 11 May 2026 to add Australia, Canada, Denmark, France, Italy, Korea, Sweden and the United Kingdom, with its own steering committee. The Critical Minerals Framework is a separate non-binding MOU. And New Clark City’s pre-existing projects have their own permits and disputes predating all of it.

Two boundary errors recur. New Clark City is in Capas and Bamban, Tarlac, not at the former Clark Air Base in Pampanga, and not in Pampanga at all. And "Pax Silica" is used interchangeably for the global initiative and the Philippine site; they have different memberships, legal statuses and risk profiles.

The core analytical error is bundling. BCDA has described the site as integrating semiconductor packaging, electronics, AI computing, R&D and mineral processing, activities that differ by an order of magnitude or more on every parameter that matters: capital intensity, jobs per dollar, water, power, hazardous waste. A single impact estimate spanning all of them is not an estimate; it is a category error. The activity mix has not been published, so every figure in circulation is unfalsifiable. BCDA’s own account has moved: on 23 July its president said the agency “may invite data centers, but it’s not all about data centers”, and that one or two of at least 30 interested firms are data-centre operators. On 6 August he said the project “is not data centers”. On 19 August BusinessWorld reported him saying the hub is “purely commercial”, will have no defence-related activities, and that no hyperscale data centres would be built for it; the Inquirer, publishing the following day, separately reported him linking that to New Clark City’s current power infrastructure being unable to sustain hyperscale facilities. Those two reports carry remarks from the same forum and are not independent corroboration. The published description in the state news agency has also changed: on 19 June PNA described the development as expected to host hyperscale data centres among other facilities, in the agency’s own descriptive wording; on 7 August it reported the BCDA president saying any data centres would serve semiconductor firms and not hyperscalers, and that major data centres would sit outside the initiative. This report records the change in the published description and does not assert that the underlying official position changed, nor whether the later statement is a clarification or a change of plan. No hyperscale restriction was found in the published project materials reviewed, including BCDA’s April proposal — a search result, not proof of absence, and no instrument yet restricts locator activity in this way.

On 24 August the account widened again, and this time from a second agency. At the House appropriations hearing on the DTI’s 2027 budget, Trade Undersecretary and BOI Vice Chairman and Managing Head Ceferino S. Rodolfo said New Clark City "is just one of the projects, and it will be focused on advanced manufacturing" and that "the whole stack of AI, we will still discuss to determine other locations for those other areas" (Manila Bulletin); pressed by ACT Teachers Rep. Antonio Tinio, that "what’s clear is, in Clark, there is no data center"; answering Akbayan Rep. Percival Cendaña, that data centres "may happen in another location" where water and electricity are more available; and that talks were held "just last week" with an unidentified Metro Manila local government about a national IC-design hub, with a Pax Silica partner that is not the United States (Inquirer). ABS-CBN renders the exclusion as "the AI data centers themselves will not be in New Clark City". Asked whether the electricity, water and environmental concerns are valid, he answered "yes, that is why we are taking inputs from everyone". No official transcript or recording of the hearing was retrieved, so each quotation is carried as its outlet’s account.

On 1 September the Palace restated the exclusion and answered the question 24 August had left open. At a Malacañang press briefing, Palace Press Officer Claire Castro said, attributing the position to the DTI, that "On the Clark Advanced Manufacturing Park, there will be no data centers", and that any investment project "whether data center or not, or whether under the Pax Silica or not, will have to undergo strict compliance with government regulations, for example, and most critically on environmental impact". Addressing possible locations elsewhere, she said "If there is talk of another location outside New Clark City, there is no proposal yet regarding this, according to DTI" (Philippine News Agency, whose rendering the English follows; the exchange was in Filipino). This materially strengthens the evidence for the government’s present stated intention that the proposed parcel will contain no data centres. It does not establish that exclusion as a formally adopted or enforceable land-use rule. The exact name Clark Advanced Manufacturing Park was not located in any proclamation, published board resolution, master plan or bid document reviewed here, although official reporting uses it for the proposed roughly 1,600-hectare development — and from 4 September 2026 so does BCDA itself, which used it throughout its own press release on the community census and, in a statement to reporters the same day, drew the distinction in its own words: CAMP is the physical development platform, while Pax Silica is the broader international partnership. That resolves whose usage the name is; it does not make it an adopted designation, and BCDA’s own release calls the park proposed throughout. So Castro’s statement does concern the proposed parcel — it simply is not an instrument establishing its legally adopted permitted uses or boundaries, and it sets no data-centre threshold, no own-use boundary, no decision-maker and no change-control rule. The 24 August and 1 September statements are compatible but address different questions: Rodolfo described a possible future location outside Clark, while Castro reported that no such proposal presently existed. Both remain in unresolved tension with the 23 July invitation statement and the 7 August own-use allowance, because no published rule defines the categories or shows whether the policy changed. Neither carrying outlet’s headline is on this site’s news rail: BusinessWorld’s substituted "outside Clark" for Castro’s narrower "outside New Clark City", and BusinessMirror’s added "formal" to "no proposal yet" while its lede read that as no company having formally applied. The finding is unchanged: the formally adopted activity mix of the parcel remains undeclared.

Where the assurance stops is now visible in BCDA’s own paperwork. Its July 2025 bidder information for the New Clark City ICT corridor — Annex F to Bid Bulletin No. 5 of the NCC ICT Passive Infrastructure Project — lists among the city’s industrial locators a "Hyperscale Data Center", 47.0 hectares, "construction to start on Q4 2025". PNA reported the underlying transaction in June 2024: a lease contract agreement signed alongside Tarlac Governor Susan Yap for a 47-hectare New Clark City site, for a 300 MW hyperscale facility in three 100 MW phases at about US$890 million each, US$2.7 billion in total. This review found no authoritative 2026 confirmation of that project’s construction, schedule, cancellation or current status, and nothing establishes whether the parcel lies inside or outside the proposed Pax Silica parcel; no inference is drawn either way. What it does show is that the assurance is narrower than its headline in both directions. Officials have said small locator-operated facilities for a firm’s own use may be established inside, while major ones would sit outside — and no instrument located in this review sets the threshold that separates the two, names who decides it, or says what happens if a locator’s facility grows past it. The finding is unchanged: the formally adopted activity mix of the parcel remains undeclared.

The named anchor sharpens this considerably. Foxconn’s described activity is "computer parts and electronic components manufacturing", conventional electronics assembly. Not wafer fabrication, not hyperscale compute. If the anchor sets the character of the zone, this is an electronics manufacturing park with an AI-branded name, which is a legitimate and useful thing to build but is not what the prospectus describes.

[sources drawn on: T1-05 · A-01 · A-02 · T1-37 · T1-38 · T1-39 · T1-40 · T1-44 · T3-53 · T3-54 · T3-56]

### 07. Research methodology and limitations
A triangulated, mixed-method design, and the things it cannot see.

The design combines a systematic scoping search; a four-tier source hierarchy with explicit adjudication of conflicts; process tracing against a ten-step implementation ladder; a claim-evidence audit; parametric techno-economic appraisal with disclosed formulas; legal-textual analysis; environmental and social risk screening under Philippine law; stakeholder and distributional mapping; comparative case analysis; and scenario and sensitivity analysis.

This review is not PRISMA-compliant and is not described as such. No protocol was pre-registered, no dual independent screening was performed, and no formal risk-of-bias instrument was applied. Wikipedia was consulted only to cross-check dates; several of its details conflicted with State Department primary sources and were discarded.

Four adjudication rules are visible throughout. Primary text beats characterisation. Official statistical series beat industry association claims. A party’s admission against interest carries extra weight, the Finance Secretary’s "thousands of jobs" is treated as more probative than aggregate promotional figures. Silence from a party with an interest in speaking is weak corroboration only, and never bears weight alone. And technical claims are tested against arithmetic, not against the credibility of the claimant.

Known limitations: the public record includes the core offer/Declaration/BOI-published reply and additional official instruments, but Annex A and an executed zone framework remain unlocated. No independent fieldwork was conducted. Direct community statements carried by media and advocacy-mediated accounts are distinguished; neither supplies a validated parcel baseline. Conditional Capas/Bamban positions, provincial remarks and August consultation are recorded. Formal municipal correspondence, consultation minutes/submissions, Sanggunian resolutions and parcel/FPIC records remain the specific gaps.

[sources drawn on: T1-01 · T2-01 · T3-14]

### 08. Detailed timeline
Nine months from initial discussion to a published unilateral offer and a conditional US acceptance in principle, with no executed zone agreement located.

The enabling statutes come first: RA 7227 created BCDA in 1992; CREATE MORE was signed in November 2024; RA 12252 replaced the 50+25-year foreign investor lease with a single term of up to 99 years in September 2025. Aeta Hungey groups filed CADT applications over Capas in 1999, 2014 and May 2019. New Clark City construction began in 2018.

The initiative itself moved quickly. The inaugural Pax Silica Summit was held in Washington on 12 December 2025, with seven founding signatories, the US, Japan, Israel, Australia, Singapore, Korea and the UK, and the Netherlands, Taiwan, Canada, the EU and OECD attending as guests. The Netherlands associated as a non-signing partner five days later; Qatar and the UAE signed in mid-January, India on 20 February, Sweden in March, Finland in April and Norway in May. On 2 February 2026 the US launched Project Vault, and on 4 February Secretary Rubio launched FORGE at the inaugural Critical Minerals Ministerial, the same event at which DENR Secretary Lotilla signed the US-Philippines Critical Minerals MOU. On 9 April 2026 BCDA President Joshua Bingcang signed the proposal letter offering roughly 4,000 acres rent-free for two years. On 16 April 2026 the Philippine Embassy transmitted it by Note Verbale, DTI Usec. Rodolfo signed the Declaration, and the State Department announced the Zone, "joint governance," and an intent to "fuse American expertise in institutions and legal regimes."

Then contestation. On 18 May 2026 Bingcang stated the Philippines had refused a US request to place the zone under American law; on 25 May Helberg called that "patently untrue"; on 26 May the State Department declined to say what governing law would apply. On 17 June Reps. Tinio, Elago and Co filed House Resolution 1128, calling for an investigation in aid of legislation into Philippine participation and the establishment of the Economic Security Zone; it was read on 28 July and has been pending with the Committee on Economic Affairs since 11 August. Three more followed in a week: Akbayan’s House Resolution 1227 on 28 July, Rep. Pimentel’s House Resolution 1231 the same day, directing the Special Committee on Strategic Intelligence to hold a briefing with the defence and security agencies, and House Resolution 1247 on 29 July from Reps. Erice, Lagman, San Fernando, De Jesus and De Lima, putting eleven questions including the legal authority under which the agreement was executed. All four were read by 3 August and all four remain pending in committee. At the Second Summit in late June, the Under Secretary’s opening remarks of 25 June previewed the Zone in a dedicated section, and the outcomes document published the following day did not mention it.

The final fortnight compressed everything. Foxconn was named on 7 July. The DFC approved LNG feasibility funding on 16 July. Scientists and farmers marched to the US Embassy on 13 July. Job claims escalated across four agencies between 22 and 26 July. And on 24 July the USTR imposed a 12.5% tariff and the peso closed at a record low. The signed or enacted legal measures identified in the retrieved record include Philippine enabling statutes, a separate ACWA Power solar lease, the US–Philippine Philippines Energy Threshold Program grant instrument signed on 10 September 2026, and a US tariff applicable to Philippine exports. The tariff is an external trade measure, not an instrument of this project. This report previously presented its list of binding instruments as exhaustive and omitted the signed threshold-program instrument; that is corrected here.

What comes next is dated. The inaugural Luzon Economic Corridor Investment Forum opened in Taguig on 10 September 2026, scheduled for 10 and 11 September, co-hosted by the governments of the United States, the Philippines and Japan and sponsored by USTDA. Two PCO accounts of the President’s keynote located in this review contain no occurrence of "Pax Silica"; that is a bounded statement about those published pages, not every forum session or untranscribed remark. One PCO account names Australia, Canada, Denmark, France, Italy, the Republic of Korea, Sweden and the UK as partner countries; INQUIRER.net quotes the President on moving further into semiconductor design, research and engineering and developing the critical-minerals sector responsibly and strategically. The host governments’ release, as reproduced by SunStar, announced Spain and the European Union as additions to the corridor partnership, although USTDA had already listed the EU as a partner in August and the sources retrieved do not say whether September marked formal admission or establish either addition’s legal form. GMA News quoted US Ambassador Lee Lipton referring to US–Philippine work in New Clark City on semiconductors, AI and trusted technologies; the PCO’s account of his remarks used similar sectoral language without naming New Clark City. Although Ambassador Lipton linked New Clark City to prospective investment in semiconductors, AI and trusted technologies, no retrieved host-government release identifies the forum itself, or any agreement announced or signed there, as a Pax Silica event or proposed-zone instrument. The two governments also signed the US$60 million Philippines Energy Threshold Program, which the Department of Finance calls a Millennium Challenge Corporation Threshold Program Grant Agreement, and USTDA-funded corridor activities were announced; none was identified in the releases retrieved as a Pax Silica or proposed-zone instrument, and the agreement text was not located, so its obligations have not been reviewed here. Outside, a protest directed by its organisers against Pax Silica and the LEC forum became a physical confrontation with police: later reports placed arrests at five, with differing rosters; a later Philstar report narrows but does not resolve the discrepancy. Manila Bulletin reported on 11 September that the Southern Police District initially reported 43 police officers and five activists injured; SunStar had separately attributed the same figures to SPD deputy director Col. Robert Baesa on 10 September. Manila Bulletin further reported that the National Capital Region Police Office later said its "latest validation" showed 16 PNP personnel with minor injuries. No underlying SPD or NCRPO record was located. The 43 is therefore retained only as an initial SPD figure reported by those outlets and is not adopted; 16 is carried as NCRPO’s subsequently reported figure, not as an independently verified medical total. Philstar attributed 16 injured officers to the same official, and why the figures attributed to him differ is not established. The PNA copy gives 16 officers and five activists; organisations reported 23 to at least 27 injured protesters. The same-population protester counts remain unreconciled. The PNP said its officers exercised maximum tolerance; the organisations present condemned what they called a violent dispersal. A PNA report available through one republishing outlet, Republika News, quoted SPD chief Brig. Gen. Rodel Pastor as saying police intended to file cases against those arrested, organisers and Bayan Muna chairperson Teddy Casiño. No primary SPD recording or transcript, independent carrier, complaint, prosecutor’s filing or court record was located in the reviewed evidence. This establishes only the police official’s reported announcement as to Casiño and other organisers. Manila Bulletin subsequently reported an inquest and bail recommendation concerning the five arrested respondents, but no retrieved record establishes that a complaint was filed against Casiño or that any offence occurred. On 12 September Manila Bulletin reported that, following inquest proceedings, the Taguig City Office of the Prosecutor issued what the outlet described as a certification recommending bail of ₱60,000 for each of the five people arrested on 10 September—₱300,000 in total—in relation to alleged violations of Articles 148, 151, 153 and 155 of the Revised Penal Code. The underlying certification, complaints, inquest resolution and any court information were not located, and when this passage was first written, on 13 September, no second carrier had been found. A reported bail recommendation after inquest is a procedural development, not a finding that an offence occurred, proof that an information was filed in court, or evidence that bail was posted or the respondents released. No retrieved record shows a complaint filed against Teddy Casiño. RMN, attributing the arrests to the PNP’s public information office, reported only that inquest proceedings were under way on 11 September. On 14 September Philstar reported, expressly attributing its account to the human-rights group Karapatan, that the five—whom it described as paralegals—had each posted ₱60,000 bail on 12 September and had been released from detention; it said three were arrested during the protest outside the hotel and two after going to the Tuktukan police station in Taguig. Philstar’s description of bail posted "before the Taguig City prosecutor’s office" does not identify a court, a judicial approval, a bail receipt or a release order, and no police, prosecutor’s-office or court confirmation was located, so the posting and the release remain Karapatan’s account as carried by one outlet; the ₱60,000 amount agrees with Manila Bulletin’s earlier report of the recommendation. Posting bail is not an admission or a finding that an offence occurred, and it does not by itself establish whether an information was filed in court. Philstar’s 14 September roster—Mara Peralta, Jona Yang, Kenneth Castor, RC Placido and Daya Juliano—agrees with TV5’s Karapatan-attributed roster except for Castor/Castro and differs from Philstar’s own earlier list; because the two agreeing lists derive from Karapatan, their agreement is not independent corroboration, and the discrepancy is narrowed, not resolved. On 11 September Palace Press Officer Claire Castro, speaking at a briefing in New Delhi, urged opponents to take their objections to the appropriate agencies and criticised conduct she associated with violence. "Proper protest uses reason and intelligence. Please engage with the appropriate agencies so they can understand what you are advocating for," she said, according to Inquirer. Philippine News Agency independently reported the New Delhi briefing and characterised her appeal as one for peaceful dialogue rather than violence. On 11 September protesters opposing Pax Silica and the LEC assembled at Bayanihan Park in Angeles City and marched toward the Clark Freeport Zone’s main gate, where they held a program; participants later travelled by vehicle to Capas, Tarlac (Inquirer; Punto Central Luzon). Inquirer and a separate photo report described attendance as several hundred, but no documented count was located. The same day in Iloilo City, youth groups led by the League of Filipino Students–Panay picketed outside the University of the Philippines Visayas Iloilo City campus, calling for rejection of Pax Silica and Executive Order No. 122 on the mining and critical-minerals sector, among other demands (Daily Guardian). Panay News described an 11 September LFS-led protest at the nearby Infante flyover involving youth, farmers, women and other progressive groups. The matching date, organiser, subject and adjacent locations make it likely that the two reports concern the same mobilisation, but neither report expressly establishes that identity. Participants also invoked the proposed private AI data centre in Oton, Iloilo, which its proponent withdrew in August; no official document located designates that proposal as part of Pax Silica. Iloilo Governor Arthur Defensor Jr. had separately floated an "Iloilo version" of Pax Silica on 12 August, but no retrieved government decision, project instrument or site designation establishes an approved Pax Silica project on Panay. Neither report supplied a documented attendance count or estimate. At what Context.ph reported as a press conference on Thursday, 10 September, Ambassador Heather Variava, the US Senior Advisor for Economic, Energy, and Business Affairs, said: "The Luzon Economic Corridor…is an initiative that is separate from Pax Silica, although they are indeed connected" (Context.ph). At what The Manila Times reported as a virtual briefing on Friday, 11 September, she said that "any agreements that we come to meet the legal requirements of both—in this case, both the United States and the Philippines" (The Manila Times). No recording or transcript was located for either quotation; because the two outlets’ accounts overlap in some reported remarks, the retrieved record does not establish whether they describe one appearance or two, and the quotations are kept separately attributed. Neither report establishes which sense of "Pax Silica" she meant: the name is that of the international State Department initiative, but Context.ph placed the remark amid concerns about Pax Silica projects around New Clark City. Either way, an official’s reported remark does not legally delineate the proposed New Clark City zone or hub, which Philippine official communications have also called "Pax Silica" and described as "under the Luzon Economic Corridor"; if her referent was the proposed hub, the remark stands in unresolved tension with that description. The second is a prospective official assurance, not an agreement or legal analysis; it establishes neither the legal form nor the present compliance of any project-level instrument. Daily Tribune reported that, at an afternoon press conference during the 10 September forum, Finance Undersecretary Angela Ignacio said: "For now, it may be premature to be talking about Pax Silica because it’s really a work in progress." It separately reported Ambassador Variava as saying: "This is an agreement that’s under deliberation, so it’s premature to comment on the details." Both quotations were located only in Daily Tribune’s reporting; Context.ph independently places Variava at a Thursday press conference but does not carry those words. Ignacio expressly referred to Pax Silica, but neither report identifies the particular unfinished instrument, arrangements or project details under discussion, and the antecedent of Variava’s "this agreement" is not established by a transcript. The Philippines had already signed the non-binding Pax Silica Declaration on 16 April 2026. The remarks therefore provide single-carrier evidence that further Pax Silica-related details or arrangements remained under deliberation; they do not identify the legal form or status of a project-level instrument, independently establish KJ-16, or confirm, move or abandon the reported November target. As of 12 September, November remained an official target under consideration rather than a confirmed signing date: BCDA President Bingcang said on 19 August that it was not set in stone, and DTI Undersecretary Rodolfo reportedly reiterated on 28 August that the timetable could change if negotiations were not ready. Reports published on 14 and 15 September appear to draw on the same press encounter with Trade Undersecretary Rodolfo associated with the 10–11 September Luzon Economic Corridor Investment Forum; the exact date of his remarks was not established. BusinessMirror reports him describing the contemplated instrument as a master agreement between BCDA and an unnamed US counterpart, rather than one signed directly by the Philippine and US governments. Manila Bulletin, The Manila Times and Philstar report continued optimism about signing in November, subject to safeguards or continuing consultation. The carriers differ on the contemplated structure: BusinessMirror places the US counterpart on "the development side"; The Manila Times calls it a "co-developer and partner"; and Manila Bulletin alone reports that the agreement covers a lease of the property to a US agency. No instrument text, draft, term sheet, transcript, DTI or BCDA release identifying the master agreement, or US confirmation was located, so its legal form, parties and legal effects at signature remain unestablished.

[sources drawn on: T1-10 · T1-11 · T1-02 · T1-05 · T1-07 · T1-06 · T3-06 · T3-03 · T1-26 · T1-35 · T1-36 · T1-37 · T1-38 · T1-39 · T1-40 · T1-43 · T1-44 · T3-35 · T3-36 · T3-37 · T3-38 · T3-39 · T3-40 · T3-41 · T3-42 · T3-43 · T1-41 · T3-44 · T3-45 · T3-46 · T3-47 · T3-48 · T3-49 · T3-50 · T3-51 · T3-52 · T3-53 · T3-54 · T3-55 · T3-56 · T3-76 · T3-77 · T3-78 · T3-79 · T3-80 · T3-81 · T3-83 · T3-84 · T3-85 · T3-86 · T3-87 · T3-88 · T1-57 · T3-90]

### 09. Global Pax Silica structure and objectives
A State Department programme, not an international organisation.

Pax Silica has no secretariat with legal personality, no founding treaty, no published shared budget, no dispute-resolution mechanism, no accession criteria and no exit provisions. Coordination runs through the Office of the Under Secretary for Economic Affairs, held by Jacob Helberg, previously Senior Advisor to the CEO of Palantir, Google’s global lead for foreign-interference product policy, and a Commissioner on the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission. This is not a neutral trade-facilitation background, and Pax Silica is best understood as an instrument of technology-bloc formation, which is exactly how its own fact sheets describe it.

The Declaration’s operative language is uniformly hortatory: affirm, recognize, believe, encourage, seek, support, understand, and at its strongest, intend. "Intend" is the standard marker of a deliberately non-binding instrument. There is no "shall," no obligation, no entry-into-force provision, no termination clause and no dispute settlement. The legal reading cuts both ways: the Philippines has not surrendered sovereignty by signing, but equally none of the benefits invoked in Manila is secured by it. A second government has now put the same reading on the record: on 2 September 2026 the Lithuanian government approved joining the Declaration, and its foreign ministry said in doing so that the instrument is not an international treaty and would create no legal obligations for Lithuania under international or national law. That is an interested characterisation, since it is also what lets an executive join without ratification, and it is carried here as corroboration of the reading above rather than as its foundation.

There were 24 signatories as of 26 June 2026, the 23 listed on the State Department’s own Pax Silica page plus the United States, which the page omits from its own list. Italy signed at Brindisi on 31 July 2026 as the 25th signatory, bringing the standing count to 25. Taiwan endorses the principles without signing, through a separate joint statement. A different and larger group of 35 economies signed the Joint Statement on AI Opportunity, several of them not Pax Silica signatories. Lithuania, one of that group, approved joining the Declaration itself on 2 September 2026, but that is an approval to join and not an accession: no executed instrument, Lithuanian signature announcement or State Department welcome note had been located as at 3 September 2026, so the standing count stays at 25. The Board of Investments publishes the signed declaration recording that the Philippines and the United States signed that statement at Washington on 25 June 2026; its signature blocks are redacted, so the signatories cannot be identified from it. Media have variously reported 13, 14, 15, 23, 24, "close to three dozen" and "about 30," and at least one Philippine outlet has listed Saudi Arabia, which the State Department list does not support. One signatory, the European Union, is not a country. Officials should stop using "member countries" without qualification.

In seven months the initiative has delivered four things: the Declaration; the Joint Statement; a funding opportunity for an AI supply-chain provenance platform, described in earlier reporting as piloted in Panama; and the Stanford Foundry School.

CORRECTION, 16 Aug 2026. This section called that funding opportunity planned until today. It was not. This site’s own news rail carried the State Department’s notice on 13 August 2026, verified and published, three days before this section was updated — two surfaces of the same document disagreeing for three days. Two things the rail item said are also restated here: US$50m is the register’s award maximum, not an established programme total, and the posted synopsis does not mention Panama.

The funding notice, now posted. It is the Pax Silica Artificial Intelligence Assistance Project, number DFOP0019193, from the State Department’s Bureau of Economic and Business Affairs under Assistance Listing 19.322, Economic Statecraft. State listed it on 12 August 2026; the federal grants register shows version 2 posted 14 August, with applications closing 20 August. An earlier version exists whose posting date this report could not retrieve, so nothing should be inferred about the length of the application window. The instrument is a cooperative agreement, with three expected awards between US$1m and US$50m and a blank total-award field, so the register establishes no programme total; no cost sharing, open only to for-profit organisations other than small businesses. Its object is a trusted supply-chain credentialing and provenance platform and a "Silicon Highway", a digital-physical corridor with cryptographic cargo verification, and it describes itself as leveraging foreign assistance from the "Pax Fund", a name for which no published State Department authority, appropriation, size or governance document could be located. Only the public synopsis was read, not the full announcement, so no conclusion is drawn about which partner economies it names. One of the four deliverables is therefore no longer purely informational. But a solicitation is not a facility, no award has been located, and an award of US$1–50m sits roughly three to five orders of magnitude below the US$40–70bn BCDA says the New Clark City project could attract once fully developed.

CORRECTION, 2 Aug 2026. This site previously called the Zone’s absence from the Second Summit outcomes document analytically significant, and offered two explanations, that it was not ready to be reported as a deliverable or that it is less central in Washington than in Manila. Both are withdrawn. A cross-model adversarial review established that the Under Secretary’s opening remarks of 25 June contain a dedicated Economic Security Zone section stating that the United States will announce the first Zone in the Philippines, so the Summit was not silent about it, and that neither explanation is supported by the two documents. What the record establishes is narrower, a future-tense preview on 25 June followed by omission from the formal outcomes summary on 26 June, with the documents not explaining the difference.

[sources drawn on: T1-01 · T1-06 · T1-18 · T1-41]

### 10. What the Philippines has signed, offered and obtained
One political declaration, one unilateral offer, and no enforceable zone commitment in return.

The signed Pax Silica participation instrument discussed here is the non-binding Pax Silica Declaration, on 16 April 2026, by a DTI Undersecretary. Not the President, not the Secretary of Foreign Affairs, not ratified, not transmitted to the Senate. That signature level is consistent with a non-binding instrument. It does not erase subsequent Senate scrutiny: the August hearing and September Committee-of-the-Whole decision are recorded. No Senate merits approval or concurrence, Cabinet paper or NEDA Board disposition was located in the reviewed record. If the November framework carries materially greater legal weight, it cannot properly be executed by the same route.

The BCDA letter of 9 April 2026 is a unilateral offer. It proposes a Pax Silica Coordination Office on approximately 4,000 acres under a lease-free arrangement for two years as the Philippines’ in-kind contribution. Section I lists five coordination functions, minerals supply-chain security, joint strategic industrial planning, allied investment mobilisation, workforce development and technology transfer, and such other activities as the two governments may determine. Section II.3 restricts the entire 4,000 acres to those purposes exclusively.

The United States replied, and the reply is now in the record. A letter published by the Philippine Board of Investments, dated 16 April 2026 and bearing Jacob S. Helberg’s typed name beneath a redacted signature, records a conditional acceptance in principle of the two-year rent-free lease — subject to confirmation of the site and boundaries, and to conclusion of an appropriate lease agreement. Funding, construction and operations are deferred to separate arrangements, subject to US law and the availability of funds, so the letter itself records no US funding commitment. Two cautions belong with it. Its US authorship and execution are not independently authenticated: the signature is redacted, and no State Department copy, release or archived contemporaneous copy was located. And later statements from both governments show the long-term framework and final contract still under negotiation, so this is an acceptance in principle rather than a concluded arrangement. The letter also describes the land as a Coordination Office, while Philippine announcements frame the same acreage as an industrial acceleration hub; no inference is drawn that the United States excluded the wider hub, only that the documents do not describe it consistently.

Seven problems appear on the face of the offer. The exclusive-use clause contradicts the public project. Annex A is missing. No lease term is stated. The Year-3 rate is "to be discussed." Section III rests the offer on RA 7916, the Special Economic Zone Act of 1995, and then miscites the BCDA charter as Republic Act No. 7277, the Magna Carta for Disabled Persons, rather than RA 7227; US acceptance is to be effected under 22 U.S.C. §2697 and the Foreign Affairs Manual. The letter reserves consultations on "the status of personnel" and "internal security", and "status of personnel" is the standard formulation in status-of-forces and status-of-mission instruments, so it was the Philippine document itself that placed the subject on the table. And BCDA proposes to enter the Supplemental Agreement "on behalf of the Philippine Government," which is a government-owned corporation acting as the state’s treaty-adjacent agent.

No enforceable commitment to implement the proposed zone was located in the reviewed record. The separate signed MCC energy threshold grant is acknowledged in the wider bilateral record, with its text and obligations unreviewed and no identified zone-financing link. There is no investment commitment, no technology-transfer obligation, no local-content requirement, no employment floor, no wage standard, no market access, no financing facility and no trade-treatment commitment, while the same counterparty raised tariffs on Philippine goods.

[sources drawn on: T1-05 · T1-03 · T1-04 · T3-01 · T3-02 · T1-35 · T1-36 · T3-57]

### 11. New Clark City scope and implementation status
Seventeen per cent of a 9,450-hectare development, and no published map.

New Clark City is a 9,450-hectare BCDA development in Capas and Bamban, Tarlac, begun in 2018 as a disaster-resilient government and industrial centre. The Pax Silica parcel is approximately 1,618.74 hectares within it, or 17.1% of the whole.

Every substantive question about this project is downstream of a map that has not been released. Without metes and bounds, it is impossible to determine which households are affected, which watercourses are enclosed, what the catchment actually is, whether the parcel overlaps areas subject to Aeta CADT applications, or what the land is currently used for.

BCDA has confirmed this status in its own official records. On 12 May 2026, refusing a citizen’s Freedom of Information request for the project pipeline, it stated that "the project is still on the planning stage and it is premature for BCDA to release any official information," invoking the pre-decisional and premature-disclosure exceptions. On 10 June 2026 it refused a request for the site map, on the ground that records involving ongoing state negotiations and strategic master plans are not final until they are. Those two denials are the proponent’s own formal confirmation of both findings in this section: the project is pre-decisional, and the Annex A vacuum is unexplained. The May response is visibly a template, generically signed, rather than a considered policy statement. fourteen of sixteen implementation gates are open. Public discussion, including by officials, has consistently treated the project as further advanced than the record supports. The single most common category error is treating a letter of interest, a site visit, a named prospect, or a feasibility study as an investment commitment.

[sources drawn on: T1-07 · T1-15 · T3-03 · T3-08]

### 12. Governance, ownership, financing and lease structure
Joint governance is asserted; its content is undefined.

The US fact sheet describes an intent to "fuse American expertise in institutions and legal regimes" with Philippine assets under "joint governance." Neither government has published what joint governance means concretely, what body, what powers, what decision rules, what dispute mechanism, and what happens when the two legal regimes conflict. "Shared upside" is likewise undefined: there is no published equity structure, revenue-share mechanism, royalty or profit participation.

The immunity dispute is unresolved, not closed. The Wall Street Journal reported the hub would operate under US common law with embassy-equivalent protections; BCDA says it refused that request, citing RA 7652 and RA 7227 and calling it "a regular business development contract"; Under Secretary Helberg says immunity was never sought; the State Department declined to answer the direct question. The accounts reconcile if the ask was framed as "operational certainty" and the Philippine side correctly read its substance. What is not in dispute: the governing-law question is open, and the published Philippine letter expressly reserves consultations on the status of personnel and on internal security.

Land ownership is not transferred, and the reversion clause returns the property and permanently affixed improvements to the Republic on expiry. But a 99-year, sublettable, collateralisable master lease over 1,618.74 hectares held by a foreign government is a materially different proposition from thirty direct locator leases with the Philippine state, and which of the two is intended has not been disclosed.

On proposed-zone financing, no binding implementation commitment was located. The wider bilateral record separately includes the signed MCC energy threshold grant; its agreement text remains unreviewed and it is not identified as zone financing. The following older examples are technical assistance and facilities rather than zone capital: USTDA US$3.8m, raised from US$2.5m; Sweden PHP 74m; a UK export-finance capacity of PHP 411bn, which is a facility and not a project commitment; and a DFC-funded feasibility study. The one committed equity figure in the file, ACWA Power at roughly US$200m, belongs to a different project on different land. On the record searched — the State Department’s Pax Silica pages and releases, and the federal grants register — no Pax Silica financing facility, common fund or investment vehicle has been announced. CORRECTION, 16 Aug 2026. This site previously stated flatly that no such facility "exists"; that overstated what the record can show, and the finding is now scoped to the sources searched. The August 2026 funding notice does name a "Pax Fund" as its source of foreign assistance, but a name in a synopsis does not by itself establish that a constituted fund exists.

[sources drawn on: T1-05 · T3-03 · A-02 · A-03 · T1-35 · T1-36]

### 13. Technical and infrastructure feasibility
Water and power are the binding constraints, and neither has been shown soluble.

At 90 MLD, harvesting from rainfall requires a catchment of roughly 1,460–3,129 hectares depending on rainfall and runoff assumptions, between 90% and 193% of the entire site, before allowing for the 40% reserved as open space. Even under the most favourable assumptions this means capturing essentially all rainfall over essentially the whole site, which is incompatible with the stated 40% green and open space and would leave little or no parcel rainfall for groundwater recharge or for runoff to downstream flows; whether that would impair basin-wide recharge or environmental flows cannot be established by this arithmetic. At 90 MLD the proposal depends on a shared watershed resource; whether capture would reduce existing community or irrigation supply is undetermined without a basin water balance and environmental-flow analysis.

Sustaining supply through roughly 180 dry days requires 11.7–16.2 million cubic metres of storage, a major dam that appears in no published plan or cost estimate. And the 65–90 MLD figure appears to cover direct site cooling and process water only; at a benchmark of about 1.2 gallons per kWh including indirect use, a 3 GW load implies roughly 327 MLD, some 3.6 times the disclosed figure.

On 28 August 2026 the water question acquired a bidder. The BCDA Board granted original proponent status to a consortium of Maynilad Water Services Inc. and the Korea Water Resources Corporation (K-water), the operator of Angat Dam, for an unsolicited proposal reported at ₱14.8 billion to provide long-term water supply and wastewater management at New Clark City. It must still clear the public–private partnership approval process and a Swiss challenge, and BCDA’s December 2026 award date is a conditional target. Original proponent status is not a contract award, a construction commitment or evidence that the water exists. Three BCDA figures came with it, all attributed and none verified: New Clark City’s existing capacity is an estimated 20–30 MLD; estate capacity could rise to as much as 150 MLD, with the initial system designed for up to 135 MLD; and contemporaneous reporting repeated BCDA’s earlier estimate that Pax Silica could eventually require 65–90 MLD. So this one project wants between 2.2 and 4.5 times everything New Clark City can supply today, and roughly half to two-thirds of the initial designed capacity of an estate-wide system that must also serve every other user in it — offered as scale, not as an allocation, and nothing establishes that the 135 MLD would be available here. What the procurement step does not supply is the thing this section has asked for throughout. As at 1 September 2026 no water balance, catchment delineation, dry-season yield analysis, flow-duration curve, dependable drought yield, withdrawal inventory or environmental-flow reservation for this system was located in publicly available BCDA, Maynilad, K-water, NWRB or DENR-EMB material, and the announcement identifies no selected catchment. That is a publication finding rather than a claim that no such work exists — and it is precisely the point, because a December award on a proposal whose water balance has never been published would put the contract ahead of the evidence. The catchment arithmetic above is unaffected.

On power, 3,000 MW is 19.2% of the DOE’s official 15,600 MW projection for 2026 Luzon peak demand, and 20.6% of the 14,534 MW peak actually recorded by mid-2026, on a grid that ran a 373 MW deficit under red alert on 15 May 2026 with 4,106 MW unavailable to the grid, including 30 plants on forced outage. BCDA’s own signed ACWA lease sets the benchmark: 500 hectares for up to 500 MW, one hectare per megawatt. Supplying the energy of a 3,000 MW continuous load from solar needs roughly 15,000 MW of nameplate and therefore about 15,000 hectares: 9.3 times the parcel and 1.6 times the whole of New Clark City. The renewables claim is not a matter of ambition or cost; on the land available it is geometrically impossible. That impossibility is established for solar on the site and elsewhere in New Clark City at the ACWA benchmark; whether an off-site renewables-plus-firming configuration could be engineered is unknown, because no one has modelled it, including this report.

On 27 July 2026 this finding stopped resting on this report’s arithmetic alone. Energy Secretary Sharon Garin told Rappler that connecting the full 3 GW load is "too dangerous," that the grid "will just shut down" if a load that size is lost, that 100–200 MW is the manageable ceiling, and that beyond it the project will need its own power plant. The regulator that would have to approve the connection reached a consistent conclusion on grid connection independently, and went further than this report had; that is not a finding on solar land or on the eventual generation mix.

The DFC has funded a feasibility study for a ≥1,200 MW LNG terminal and plant. A US development finance institution does not fund a gas feasibility study for a project it expects to run on sunshine. Stated precisely: the LNG study is the only near-term firm-generation option on the record, not a committed plan. Three consequences go unacknowledged: BCDA’s "avoid fossil fuels" framing should be corrected; a 1,200 MW combined-cycle plant at high load factor emits on the order of 3–4 million tonnes of CO₂ a year with no published carbon accounting; and LNG is imported and dollar-denominated, creating a structural currency exposure for Philippine industrial power costs.

Positive factors, fairly stated: Clark International Airport is adjacent and handles the air freight by which semiconductors actually move. Subic Bay provides deep-water port capacity and now holds a formal, qualified role: an MOU signed on 20 July and described in BCDA’s 4 August release designates it as Pax Silica’s preferred maritime gateway, with joint studies and assessments still to follow. The agreement text is unpublished and the designation is not operational capacity. The Subic–Clark–Manila–Batangas rail corridor is progressing; New Clark City has existing trunk infrastructure. This is a genuinely well-located site. But Philippine industrial electricity at roughly 15 US cents per kWh, about 50% above Indonesia and Vietnam, and logistics at about a quarter of sales are national competitiveness problems. A zone designation does not solve them; it concentrates their consequences.

[sources drawn on: T3-12 · T3-17 · T3-26 · T2-04 · T3-06 · T1-22 · T1-23 · T3-27 · A-05 · A-06 · A-08]

### 14. Economic, employment, fiscal and industrial-policy assessment
Announced: US$40–70bn and up to a million jobs. Legally committed: zero.

Pairing US$40–70bn of capital with 130,000–190,000 direct jobs implies 134–196 jobs per developable hectare, a labour-intensive light-manufacturing density. That is not a data-centre density, not a wafer-fab density and not a refinery density. Run it in both directions: if the project is genuinely AI-native, permanent employment lands in the low tens of thousands at most; if it genuinely creates 130,000–190,000 jobs, most of that employment would have to come from assembly, test and packaging or similar labour-intensive work; if that dominated, perhaps US$15–30bn of capital would suffice, a very large conventional back-end electronics park, which is a respectable thing to build but is not what is being sold. A mixed configuration could in principle produce both figures; none has been published.

BCDA’s low-end figure of 130,000 total jobs for one 1,618.74-hectare parcel is comparable in scale to DTI-BOI’s national target of 128,000 engineers and technicians to be produced for the whole semiconductor and electronics industry by 2033 — a deadline corrected from 2028 in v2.46, BOI having published 2028 in August 2024 and 2033 repeatedly since, with no identified explanation of the change. The comparison is one of scale, not of like quantities: the target is a flow of specific occupations into the whole industry, not an employment ceiling, and not every site job requires an engineer or technician. Its high-end figure exceeds total employment across all 4,744 Subic Bay Freeport locators. The Labor Secretary’s figure would exceed the combined workforce of Subic and Clark roughly three times over. The only bottom-up figure on the record is "thousands," from the named anchor.

On the fiscal side, PHP 60bn of lease income over 25 years equals PHP 148.26 per square metre per year, with a present value of about PHP 25.6bn, 0.59% to 1.03% of the capital it is meant to host. No independent land valuation has been published, which is a governance failure independent of whether the rent is adequate. At an assumed 20% effective rate and the 160,000-job midpoint, the lower end of the PHP 68–75bn withholding tax claim implies average compensation of about PHP 2.13m per worker: 2.4 times a Philippine semiconductor engineer’s salary and 8.1 times an operator’s. The implied figure rises at a lower assumed rate and falls at a higher one, so these are explicit scenarios, not a unique implication. BCDA closed the one remaining escape route itself on 23 July 2026, describing the figure as the tax contributed by the workers, with other shares bringing the total to PHP 180bn. On that stated composition the conclusion is no longer that the fiscal case cannot be assessed, but that the tax and employment figures, as published, are not reconciled at current Philippine wage benchmarks. That does not show which figure, if either, is overstated: at fixed wages and rates fewer jobs would widen the gap, and BCDA’s under-10% foreign-worker share does not rule out a high-pay minority raising the average. Only the unpublished model can say.

Correction, 10 August 2026: earlier versions described BCDA’s US$200bn export projection as annual. New reporting places full development on an approximately 30-year horizon but does not consistently establish whether the figure is annual, cumulative over that horizon, or measured on another basis. The 2.37× comparison with one year of Philippine merchandise exports survives only as a non-period-equivalent comparison of nominal magnitudes; the projection and its temporal basis remain unsupported without the underlying study.

No published estimate exists of the cost of fiscal incentives. Under CREATE MORE, registered enterprises may take 5% SCIT or 20% CIT with enhanced deductions including a 100% additional deduction on power expenses, for up to 17 or 27 years. For a project defined by extreme electricity intensity, that is a very large tax expenditure. A project that leads with gross tax revenue while omitting tax expenditure is presenting half a ledger. Public cost per permanent job cannot presently be computed, and that it cannot be computed is itself the finding.

The genuine industrial-policy case should not be caricatured. The manufacturing gap is real and widening. The allied advantage, comparative non-entanglement with Chinese capital, is genuine and time-limited. BPO vulnerability at 7.4% of GDP makes an alternative growth engine urgent. And the country’s back-end semiconductor base is a real asset, with electronics at US$45.89bn, or 54.3%, of a US$84.48bn export book in 2025, growing 16.11% year on year. But this case argues for negotiating hard, not for accepting the current terms.

[sources drawn on: T3-09 · T3-19 · T3-23 · T3-28 · T3-29 · T1-17 · T1-19 · T2-03 · A-04 · A-07]

### 15. Legal and regulatory assessment
Executive agreement or treaty? The question has not been answered.

The Declaration is non-binding and creates no domestic legal effect. The framework agreement is the instrument that matters, and its text does not exist publicly. The threshold in Article XVIII, Section 25 of the 1987 Constitution is <em>military</em> character, so the exposure is contingent rather than established. The substance-over-form analysis rests on <em>Saguisag v. Ochoa</em> (G.R. No. 212426, 2016) and its three standards, independence from foreign control, sovereignty and applicable law, and national security, which track precisely the clauses in the published BCDA letter. Long-term exclusive foreign use, restricted access, a distinct internal security regime or dual-use functions would not by themselves make the arrangement military; Section 25 could be engaged if the framework also brought in United States military or security personnel or defence-industrial functions. As a policy recommendation, stricter than any demonstrated constitutional trigger, a framework containing those clauses should not proceed as a bare executive agreement. There is also an independent route to Senate concurrence under Article VII, Section 21.

Several statutory questions are open. Whether the Section II.3 exclusive-use clause permits private industrial locators. Whether BCDA may enter a Supplemental Agreement "on behalf of the Philippine Government." RA 7227 §5(c) does confer power to contract "with foreign government entities," but that is commercial capacity only; the Act nowhere confers power to bind the Republic as a foreign-relations act, so the open question narrows to exactly that. BCDA’s own charter term runs fifty years to about 2042 (RA 7227 §3), which sharpens rather than settles the succession question under a 99-year lease. And classification of the instrument follows substance "regardless of nomenclature" (EO 459, s. 1997, §2(a)), calling it an arrangement rather than an agreement decides nothing either way. Whether RA 12252’s 99-year lease ceiling applies at all. The regime it amends covers private lands leased by qualifying foreign investors with approved and registered investments. Although BCDA says the site will remain under BCDA ownership and Philippine jurisdiction, the land’s classification for purposes of RA 7652/RA 12252 has not been established in the public record, and the statute alone does not establish authority for a master lease to an unidentified foreign-government entity. Both points are threshold questions rather than details. Whether IPRA certification precondition and FPIC processes are engaged notwithstanding the absence of a titled CADT, under the native-title doctrine, they do not depend on a CADT having issued.

Reporting of 14–15 September attributes to Trade Undersecretary Rodolfo a description of the contemplated November instrument as a master agreement between BCDA and an unnamed US counterpart, possibly a government corporation. BusinessMirror reports him saying that it would not be signed directly between the Philippine and US governments. That reported description does not answer the open questions. An agreement signed by BCDA solely in its own corporate capacity could draw on its contracting power under RA 7227 §5(c), whereas the BCDA letter proposes that the Supplemental Agreement be entered "on behalf of the Philippine Government"; only the instrument text, parties, recitals, signature block and evidence of authority could establish the capacity in which BCDA would act. Manila Bulletin alone reports that the contemplated agreement covers a lease of the property to a US agency. If the signed instrument grants that lease—or independently grants exclusive use or another substantive land right—§23.3 requires the assessment to classify it under branch one for precautionary purposes, whatever its title. RA 12252, which applies to leases of private land by qualifying investors with approved and registered investments, would not by itself establish authority for a lease to an unidentified US government entity. No instrument text or US confirmation was located, and the counterparty and its juridical status remain unidentified.

No formal legal opinion from the DFA Office of Legal Affairs or the Office of the Solicitor General has been published on any of these questions. Publishing them is cheap and entirely within the executive’s control, though no completion time for obtaining them is established.

[sources drawn on: T1-12 · T1-13 · T1-05 · T3-01 · T3-02 · T4-04b · T3-83 · T3-84 · T3-88]

### 16. Environmental and social assessment
No project-specific EIS, water balance, energy plan, biodiversity survey or social baseline was identified in the reviewed public record.

The threshold finding is an absence. No project-specific Environmental Impact Statement, water balance study, energy plan, biodiversity survey, cumulative impact assessment or social impact assessment for the Pax Silica parcel is on the public record. DENR has stated that an EIS and Environmental Management Plan will be required, with Multipartite Monitoring Teams. None was located as a published project-specific study in the reviewed record.

The cumulative dimension is the one most likely to be missed. An assessment scoped to the parcel boundary would exclude the ACWA solar site, the LEC rail corridor, the LNG terminal and plant, the proposed Subic–Clark jet-fuel pipeline, and any upstream mining expansion, which together are the actual footprint.

On indigenous rights, BCDA’s position that no ancestral domain is affected rests on the absence of a titled domain, not the absence of a claim. Aeta Hungey CADT applications over Capas were filed in 1999, 2014 and May 2019, and displacement disputes at New Clark City have run since 2018. The dispute over affected households, BCDA’s "about 10 farmers" against campaigners’ ~20,000 Aeta and farmers, is unresolvable without Annex A; the two figures are almost certainly describing different footprints. On-site reporting published 18 August 2026 adds a departure account the hearing record did not contain: two residents of Sitio Sapang Kawayan said they were told they could be required to leave by December, one recalling only until Christmas, with no relocation destination or assistance communicated to them and payment said to cover their houses but apparently not the land. That is reported testimony, not an agency record — no corresponding BCDA notice, valuation schedule, relocation plan or demolition order has been published. The commission announced on 20 August 2026 that it had conducted or begun a census and validation of Aeta Hungey households at that sitio, following its chairperson’s stated intention at the 14 August Senate hearing to obtain an exact validated count; the reporting carrying that announcement appears largely derivative of it, and no household, family or person total, boundary, method or reference date has been published.

On 31 August 2026 the opposition acquired a name and a single structure. The Network Opposed to Pax Silica was launched in Quezon City as a multi-sectoral alliance of civil-society, religious, scientific, farmer, student and environmental organisations seeking to halt the initiative. At the launch Petronila Capiz-Muñoz, identified as chieftain of the Aeta community at Sitio Sapang Kawayan, told reporters that residents had learned of the project through social media, that there had been no consultation, and that they had again been told to leave, this time by December, and said the development threatened their community, livelihood, church and burial ground. This is attributed testimony and nothing more. Its weight is that it carries, from the chieftain herself at a public event and in more than one outlet, the same December-or-Christmas account this report has held since 18 August from two other residents. It establishes no official or documented deadline; the quotations reached English through translation; BCDA’s contrary position stands, and displacement remains disputed. It is an alliance launched by its participating groups, and nothing here establishes registration, membership numbers or representativeness.
