A school-level position is recorded on the same footing as the church-labour one and is not counted in the coalition (v2.56, added seven weeks late as a correction of a coverage omission rather than as a new development): the Philippine Daily Inquirer reported that St Scholastica’s Academy, a Catholic Benedictine school in the City of San Fernando, Pampanga, issued a statement on 25 July 2026 which, while recognising the project’s potential to spur economic growth, sought transparency and a moratorium on implementation until environmental, social and governance concerns are adequately addressed, and independent scientific assessments of projected water and energy consumption, saying no publicly available comprehensive Environmental Impact Assessment, no complete disclosure of long-term water and energy requirements and no full accounting of effects on host communities and neighbouring provinces including Pampanga had been published. No primary copy of the statement and no independent carrier was located, so its date, contents and quotations rest on that one report, and 25 July is the article’s "On Saturday" read against a Monday publication. It is a school’s institutional statement, not a diocesan or bishops’-conference position. Pampanga is a neighbouring, not the host, province, and no claim is made that this was the first institutional position from Pampanga.

On 1 September 2026 a cabinet department said its own assessment is unfinished. At the House budget briefing on the Department of Agriculture’s 2027 budget, Gabriela Women’s Party Rep. Sarah Elago asked whether the department had assessed the project’s effects, citing reports that around 15,000 farmers and up to 20,000 Aeta people could lose their livelihoods and ancestral lands. Agriculture Secretary Francisco P. Tiu Laurel Jr. answered "Right now, we are still thoroughly assessing the full effects of Pax Silica. The initial reports I have seen indicate that not that many people will be affected. But our assessment is not yet finished", added "From what I understand from what I see on TV, within the 1,600-hectare Clark area, it doesn’t seem like there are that many directly affected farmers. I really cannot say as of now until our study comes out on what the effects will be on agriculture", and, asked when it would be done, said "Perhaps, in another 30 days". The exchange was in Filipino and the English follows GMA News’s rendering; the Inquirer rendered portions differently, puts the farmer figure at approximately 15,200, and does not carry the Aeta figure. No DA administrative order, terms of reference, scope, method, team, completion date or commitment to publish was located in this review, so the thirty days is a tentative estimate given under questioning and not a written or publicly documented departmental timetable. This preserves the finding that the affected-household count is unknown while adding mixed evidence about the competing claims: the unfinished assessment reinforces the uncertainty, and the Secretary’s repeated preliminary impression points directionally toward the lower end of the dispute and away from the campaigners’ cited figures, but it verifies no figure because he supplied no count or completed method. Rep. Elago’s figures are her characterisation of third-party reports and are not adopted here.

An agriculture-industry group’s reported representative stated conditions rather than opposition. BusinessMirror reported on 14 September 2026 that Jayson Cainglet, executive director of the Samahang Industriya ng Agrikultura (SINAG), said the group was not opposed to investment or economic diversification but that "Pax Silica and other projects must not be pursued by sacrificing the country’s agricultural production capacity and rural livelihoods". According to BusinessMirror, Cainglet called for projects under Pax Silica or similar initiatives to be preceded by an impact assessment, comprehensive mapping of potentially affected farms and agricultural areas, no displacement of agricultural livelihoods, a clear legal guarantee prioritising agricultural and household water requirements over industrial requirements, continuous independent monitoring of groundwater, irrigation water, soil and surrounding agricultural areas, and a legally enforceable mechanism allowing government to reduce, suspend or stop operations causing serious or irreversible harm. When this paragraph was first written, on 14 September, no original SINAG statement, transcript or second carrier had been located. BusinessWorld reported the same day a statement from Cainglet with substantially overlapping content and wording, including "Pax Silica must proceed — but not at the expense of agricultural land, irrigation water, farmers’ livelihoods, environmental quality, and food security", and adding a call to prohibit converting agricultural land for such projects (updated in v2.55). The overlap suggests that both outlets drew on one distributed statement, so the second report corroborates that the statement was issued rather than supplying an independent account; no SINAG original was located, and 14 September remains a publication date, not an established date of the remarks. SINAG is not counted in the opposition coalition: this is recorded as Cainglet’s conditional position as attributed by BusinessMirror, and the concerns are not treated as findings of actual or prospective harm. It does not alter the finding that the number of affected households is unknown. In the same BusinessWorld report, former Agriculture Secretary William D. Dar, speaking to BusinessWorld via Viber, said the project should be powered by renewable energy, build rainwater catchment and water-recycling facilities, and properly resettle affected farmers and communities before development begins, adding: "Without these assurances then this initiative must not go forward"; he also said it would not affect agricultural production if properly done with mitigation. Dar’s remarks rest on BusinessWorld alone; he holds no current office, and his position is recorded as conditional, not counted in the opposition coalition, and not treated as a finding of prospective harm.

The local government record was never as thin as this report said, and one of its own findings was overstated. Between 11 and 19 August 2026 three things entered the record that this report had not carried. Capas Mayor Roseller Rodriguez wrote to President Marcos and to BCDA on 11 August invoking Sections 26 and 27 of the Local Government Code, saying the municipality would withhold support until BCDA held a meaningful public consultation — not supporting, not opposing until one happens. Acting Bamban Vice Mayor Levy Tadeo then named Aeta communities in five sitios of Barangay Anupul — Coop, Gayaman, Malasa, Mabilog and Mainang — as overlapping the project, a second affected-community locus alongside Sitio Sapang Kawayan in Capas, while Governor Christian Tell Yap welcomed the jobs and investment. On 19 August BCDA and the provincial government held a consultation at the Tarlac Convention Center, the most substantial proponent-led local engagement in this record. A correction follows, and it runs against this report: the finding that no project-specific consultation record had been published is withdrawn as overstated, because BCDA has published a dated account of that consultation. What survives is narrower and still true — no minutes, attendance list, submissions, issues-and-responses register, grievance mechanism, compensation framework, livelihood restoration plan or independent monitoring arrangement has been published. And the two published accounts of the same meeting do not record the same meeting: BCDA’s names no speaker, objection or demand, while contemporaneous local reporting the next day records the Capas and Concepcion mayors, the acting Bamban vice mayor and Roberto Calara Mallari, Roman Catholic Bishop of Tarlac, pressing unanswered questions on water, power, displacement and ancestral domain. That is a divergence in the published record, not a finding of concealment. None of it is a consent process: no account of 19 August identifies an indigenous representative, NCIP participation or any FPIC step.

On hazardous materials, semiconductor and refining chemistry generates acids, solvents, fluorinated gases, tailings and residues. No treatment, storage and disposal plan has been published, and the former base lands at Subic and Clark have a documented contamination history. Financial assurance bonds and environmental liability insurance sized to remediation cost are the standard response and are absent.

[sources drawn on: T3-16 · T3-17 · T2-06 · T4-05 · T1-20 · A-11 · A-12 · T3-35 · T3-36 · T3-37 · T3-38 · T3-42 · T3-43 · T3-46 · T3-50 · T3-51 · T3-52 · T3-76 · T3-79 · T3-80 · T3-81 · T3-82 · T3-89 · T3-90]

### 17. Geopolitical, sovereignty and national-security implications
A strategy of displacement, stated by its author, hosted physically by the Philippines.

The US fact sheet is unusually explicit: the Luzon hub is intended as the first Zone in a broader industrial network, and that network is described as capable of competing with, and ultimately displacing, the concentrated supply chains on which the world currently depends. That is the mission statement of the enterprise the Philippines has agreed to host first. It is a source of both leverage and exposure.

A reported instance, and its limits. Reuters, in a wire carried by CNBC on 15 August 2026 and by GMA News in Manila on 16 August, reported that the State Department has prepared a draft letter to the 35 signatories of the Joint Statement on AI Opportunity, the Philippines among them, warning that they will be excluded from Pax Silica if they also sign up for a competing framework. The draft states that signature of the Declaration "is not merely a membership subscription, but a commitment" and "cannot be held alongside membership in duplicative initiatives whose expectations conflict with our own." Reuters reports the letter does not specifically mention China; the competing framework it identifies is the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization, whose establishing agreement China’s foreign ministry records as signed by representatives of 29 countries on 16 July 2026. The caveats are load-bearing and are why this moves no judgment here: the draft is undated and unsent, Reuters could not determine when or whether it would go out or in what form, the State Department declined to comment on "purportedly leaked internal documents", and the account rests on one news organisation, one anonymous official and a document this report has not seen; the many republications are the same wire copy, not corroboration. As reported it is an internal draft, not announced United States policy. No express exclusivity or incompatibility clause appears in either instrument the Philippines has signed. The narrow question this raises is answerable in the framework text: whether participation is stated to impose any restriction on the Philippines joining other countries’ AI or supply-chain initiatives.

What four governments have since published. Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development records that on 25 June 2026, in Washington, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister Zhaslan Madiyev signed the Declaration of Accession of the Republic of Kazakhstan to Pax Silica, and that Kazakhstan thereby officially joined. Three weeks later, on 16 July 2026 in Shanghai, Kazakhstan signed the agreement establishing China’s World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization: a Xinhua report on China’s government portal records representatives of 29 countries including Kazakhstan signing it, making their countries WAICO’s founding members, and Indonesia’s Coordinating Ministry for Economic Affairs published the list of signatory states the same day. Among the 29 states Indonesia names, Kazakhstan is the only one that also appears on the 25-participant Pax Silica roster this assessment uses; Oman signed the WAICO agreement and is not a Pax Silica signatory. Separately, on 9 September 2026 Singapore’s Ministry of Digital Development and Information published a parliamentary reply confirming that Singapore, one of the seven original Declaration signatories, has received a WAICO invitation and will consider it, and that there is no ASEAN position on either WAICO or Pax Silica. What this establishes is a sequence and nothing more: participation in Pax Silica did not prevent Kazakhstan from signing WAICO’s establishing agreement before Reuters publicly reported the draft warning. Signature, ratification, entry into force and operative membership are not interchangeable, and this assessment has not seen the WAICO agreement, so Kazakhstan’s position there is recorded as signature and a founding-member designation by Chinese official sources, not as accession or established legal membership. The draft letter is undated, so the conduct predates the reporting of it, not demonstrably the draft. Nothing here shows United States knowledge, approval, acquiescence or non-enforcement, nothing corroborates that the draft was authentic, sent or adopted, and nothing bears on the Philippines: neither case speaks to Manila’s invitation status, its policy, or what it would do. No judgment, confidence level or scenario weight moves. Added v2.51.

The counterparty relationship is asymmetric in a way the framing obscures. The Philippines is being asked to grant durable, specific, physical concessions, land, water, power, rent forgone, in exchange for a non-binding declaration and feasibility studies, by a partner that imposed an additional 12.5% tariff on Philippine exports on 24 July 2026.

The claim that the project is purely commercial is not sustainable as stated. The Philippine Ambassador to the United States has publicly linked Pax Silica revenue to the country becoming "more militarily equipped." That establishes a strategic-security linkage, not an on-site defence function. No dual-use exclusion clause is published, and no national security assessment of concentrating strategic assets near Clark and existing EDCA sites has been published either.

China has twice demonstrated willingness to use rare-earth export controls as leverage, and Philippine agricultural exports are a soft and historically used pressure point. Keeping the Zone genuinely multilateral, with Japanese, Korean and European participation, is both a commercial and a geopolitical hedge.

[sources drawn on: T1-03 · T3-01 · T3-02 · T1-18 · A-10]

### 18. Stakeholder and distributional analysis
Gains concentrate; risks distribute.

Gains concentrate in foreign investors, the national government and the construction sector. Risks concentrate in Tarlac’s water users, Luzon’s electricity consumers, Philippine taxpayers funding enabling infrastructure and incentives, and Aeta and farming households whose numbers remain unpublished.

BCDA and the executive speak frequently and are extensively documented. Affected communities are represented mainly through advocacy intermediaries. NGCP and the ERC remain conspicuously absent on project-specific interconnection and cost allocation. Local government is no longer near-absent from this record: Capas has taken a stated conditional posture — withholding support until a meaningful public consultation, formalised in an 11 August 2026 letter to the President invoking Sections 26 and 27 of the Local Government Code — Bamban’s acting vice mayor has named Aeta sitios in Barangay Anupul as overlapping the project, and the province hosted BCDA’s 19 August consultation. What is missing is the formal layer: no Sanggunian resolution, no published minutes or issues-and-responses register, and no local-government determination on the merits. That, and the unanswered Local Government Code letter, is the governance failure now. The Senate is also active without a merits position: after its 14 August Environment Committee hearing, the chamber on 8 September approved without objection a motion to constitute a Committee of the Whole for extensive discussion. The Philippine Embassy has likewise moved beyond this assessment’s former “currently passive” description by attending the Foundry School launch and publicly welcoming it as a collaboration and workforce-preparation opportunity, while identifying no Philippine participation commitment or implementation instrument. NCIP has engaged with communities and announced census work, but nothing in that record indicates initiation of the certification-precondition process.

On the critical side, the Makabayan bloc has the agenda-setting role but Akbayan’s is the more consequential critique, transparency, ownership structure, monopoly safeguards, undue foreign influence and critical-infrastructure risk. That critique is now a filed instrument: House Resolution 1227, filed on 28 July 2026 by Representatives Cendaña, Diokno and Kiram Ismula with Rep. Bag-ao, read on 3 August and referred to the Committee on Economic Affairs, where it has been pending since 11 August. It is one of four. The House’s own search index, checked on 6 September 2026, returns four numbered resolutions naming Pax Silica — 1128, 1227, 1231 and 1247 — reaching beyond the progressive blocs to a committee chairman acting on strategic-intelligence grounds and to district, labour, electric-cooperative and liberal party-list members. Filing an inquiry or briefing resolution does not by itself establish opposition, and the two instruments new to this assessment are not counted in the opposition coalition: House Resolution 1231’s recitals restate the administration’s projections approvingly. All four are pending in committee, and no substantive committee disposition was located in the House records searched. Church organisations, historically decisive in Philippine politics, are critical and have now mobilised: Caritas Philippines formally opposed the hub "in its present form" on 4 August; the Conference of Major Superiors in the Philippines wrote to the President ahead of the SONA, and religious groups joined SONA-day protests police put at around 6,000. Domestic big business, Ayala, the Makati Business Club, AmCham, is mixed rather than unaligned, and this assessment’s earlier description of it as “interested and currently unaligned” is withdrawn as to MBC and AmCham. At a Makati media get-together on 3 September 2026, reported on 6–7 September by several outlets apparently covering the same event, MBC chair Edgar O. Chua described Pax Silica and the Luzon Economic Corridor as opportunities for the country while calling for greater transparency, clearer communication and attention to environmental and employment concerns, and MBC trustee Cosette Canilao was quoted by the Manila Times saying it is “like the next revolution”. Those are reported remarks by a chair and a trustee, not a located board resolution or position paper, and they do not establish Ayala Corporation’s position. AmCham had separately welcomed the President’s call for support for the Pax Silica Industrial Hub and the Luzon Economic Corridor on 28 July 2026. No change of position by either organisation is inferred: MBC’s own 28 July commentary on the address was already partly favourable, so the date on which it adopted this position is not established here. The Manila Times reported on 11 August that SEIPI now backs the initiative and proposes a higher-value manufacturing ecosystem with infrastructure, workforce, supplier-development, incentive and environmental measures; the reported position paper was not independently retrieved, and none of its prescriptions is treated here as adopted policy or technical evidence. A new zone with preferential terms still competes with existing firms for talent and investment, which is why a competitive-neutrality review by the Philippine Competition Commission belongs in the process.

[sources drawn on: T4-01 · T4-03 · T4-04 · T4-05 · T4-07 · T3-18 · T3-11 · T3-25 · T3-30 · T1-35 · T1-36 · T3-37 · T3-38 · T3-57 · T4-04c · T4-04d · T3-90]

### 19. The public conversation: a social-listening analysis
6,437 sampled mentions, December 2025 to SONA eve. Sampled sentiment turned sharply negative by July.

Section 17 mapped who the stakeholders are; this section measures what they are actually saying. The source is a social listening export of 6,437 public mentions of "Pax Silica" worldwide from 6 December 2025 to 27 July 2026, stated by the provider to be a 10% sample excluding reshares. The figures describe those sampled mentions only. Corrected: earlier versions multiplied the sample by ten to imply about 64,000 original posts inside roughly 300,000 pieces of total activity; that population and amplification estimate is withdrawn, because the 10% rate is not independently verified and the later query inspection behind the ratio was not a benchmark of this export. The shares here are sample-dependent estimates; movements within this export on its one constant method are more informative than comparisons against figures collected differently, but remain subject to sampling and labelling error. Whether the export excluded reposts is itself unresolved: the provider’s description says so, while a later exhibit note describes the basis as repost-inclusive.

Before the Philippines joined, Pax Silica was covered, not discussed. The 2,286 pre-accession mentions were 60% online news and 28% X, with 75.2% neutral and a net of −1.0, the signature of wire-service copy. Volume moved only when a country signed, and India’s accession on 20 February was the single largest day of the whole record outside July, and net positive. Philippine-related content was 0.7% of that phase.

Accession did not just add the Philippines to the conversation; the Philippines took it over. Post-accession, 46.3% of mentions are Philippine-related and a third are in Filipino. The top channels became Facebook at 31%, X at 23% and Reddit at 23%, while news fell from 60% to 18%. Reddit went from 39 mentions to 943, a 24-fold increase. Net sentiment moved from −1.0 to −24.8.

The monthly trajectory is a structured deterioration punctuated by one recovery. April from the 16th: 181 mentions, net −3.3. May: 495, net +12.1. June: 548, net −11.7. July: 2,927, net −34.8. May’s positive spike coincides with the government’s most defensive month, the public rejection of the US jurisdiction-and-immunity request on 18 May. The apparent recovery is a temporal association in the vendor-labelled sample, not evidence of public reward or causation; the local relabelling does not reproduce it.

July was an eruption: 45% of the entire eight-month record, with the final eight days carrying 36.4% of everything ever said. July’s five biggest days fall in that window, not the entire record’s top five and all are sharply negative, 24 July at 621 mentions and net −43 as the BCDA figures blitz, the 99-year-lease disclosure and the US tariff landed together; 22 July at net −50 during Secretary Rubio’s Manila visit amid protests. The opposition has minted its own hashtag: #NoToPaxSilica appears 50 times against #PaxSilica’s 105.

Within the sample, on keyword topic categories and vendor labels, the high-volume topics are mixed: AI and technology at 41.8% of mentions sits at net −1.5, geopolitics at 20.1% sits at 0.0, jobs at 17.3% is net +2.6 and minerals at 12.3% is net +2.3. Sampled mentions on the economics run both ways. The low-volume topics are strongly negative: water and environment at net −43.8, land and indigenous rights at −50.3, governance and corruption at −54.4. Those nets describe keyword-matched sampled mentions under unvalidated machine labels, not whether the wider public debates these questions, and cells this small are sensitive to sampling and labelling error. BCDA’s July "myths vs facts" campaign was aimed precisely at the water and displacement claims, and the sampled July data show no rehabilitation of those categories. The corruption category is the smallest and the most negative of all, the theme officials have addressed least.

Four implications. The political-risk register has observed antecedents in the sample: negative mentions rose sharply in July, but the export ends on 27 July and cannot show whether that rise continued toward the November signing window. The vendor series associates February and May with better sentiment than July, but this does not establish a causal effect of assertion or disclosure, and the local labels do not reproduce the May recovery. Sampled post-accession discussion sits mainly in venues the government does not brief: within the listening platform’s coverage, Facebook, Reddit and X carry 77% of it, a third of it in Filipino, while Palace briefings remain optimised for a news channel that has fallen to 18% of sampled mentions. And four new monitoring indicators follow: monthly net sentiment on a constant method, the #NoToPaxSilica-to-#PaxSilica ratio, the channel mix, and the water and land topic share.

Caveats applied throughout: machine sentiment is unreliable on Filipino and Taglish irony, so levels are directional, and month-to-month changes on a constant method are more informative but remain subject to the same labelling error; topic categories are keyword-based and 33.3% of mentions match none; channel coverage reflects the listening platform’s access, with no TikTok and only public Facebook content; and Philippine-related and Filipino-language classifications are this report’s, not the platform’s.

Relabelling note, added v2.30. The figures in this section use the listening provider’s sentiment labels and are preserved unchanged as the record of that analysis. For the site’s running exhibit, the same 6,437 mentions were relabelled by the software that labels the daily collection, which measures sentiment toward the project among relevant mentions rather than general tone. Under that scheme the early months read strongly positive, at +24.7 to +50.7 net, where this section reads them as near-neutral wire coverage; May shows no recovery relative to April, at +39.4 falling to +28.5, so the apparent May recovery is method-dependent and establishes no causal public reward; and July’s collapse replicates almost exactly, at −35.6 against the −34.8 here. The divergences and their concordance are documented in the assessment’s v2.30 version note and Appendix H.27.

[sources drawn on: T3-13 · T3-14 · T3-15 · T4-02 · T4-08]

### 20. International comparisons and lessons
Six comparable cases. Silicon Valley is not one of them.

Foxconn in Wisconsin is not an analogy but a precedent involving the same counterparty. Announced in 2017 as US$10bn and 13,000 jobs with up to US$2.85bn in state credits; renegotiated in 2021 to US$672m and 1,454 jobs with credits cut to US$80m, but those 2021 figures are renegotiated contractual targets for tax-credit eligibility, not delivery. WEDC-verified actual delivery through 31 December 2024 is approximately US$717m invested cumulatively, 1,242 jobs and US$62.9m of credits earned. Against the original announcement that is ~7.2% of investment and ~9.6% of jobs. A November 2025 WEDC-Foxconn amendment plans a further US$569m and 1,374 jobs by 2029. The lesson is not that Foxconn is uniquely unreliable, it is that a wealthy, institutionally strong government with sophisticated counsel could not hold a large manufacturer to a headline announcement, and the only thing that protected its taxpayers was the performance-linked clawback in the contract. The Philippines has no such structure, no contract, and no clawback.

Penang shows that value-chain ascent is real but generational, driven by skills investment and supplier development rather than by zone designations or land concessions. The Philippine binding constraint is skills depth and supplier capability, not land, and a country that responds to that constraint by offering land is answering a question nobody asked.

Indonesian nickel downstreaming is the most directly transferable case: a host state that controls a scarce input can dictate terms. Indonesia used regulatory leverage over its resource, not land concessions. The Philippines holds the world’s fourth-largest copper and fifth-largest nickel and cobalt reserves, and is currently leading with the concession rather than with the lever. The counter-lesson matters too, Indonesia’s approach imposed real environmental and social costs.

India shows that even a large domestic market with deep engineering talent could not skip the back-end-first sequence. Vietnam shows that export volume without enforced local content produces thin value capture. And Intel in the Philippines, 1996–2009, is the domestic precedent: the country already hosted a marquee American semiconductor anchor for thirteen years, and neither retained it nor built a domestic chip industry from it. The capital went to Vietnam. The variable that determines whether this time differs is not the size of the announcement but whether binding technology-transfer and supplier-development obligations are written into the contract.

[sources drawn on: T1-21 · T2-01 · T1-42]

### 21. Scenario analysis
Five futures, each with a probability band of roughly ±10 points, explicit triggers and early-warning indicators.

Scenario A: proceeds substantially as announced, ~10%. Scenario B: proceeds but narrower, slower and less capital-intensive, ~35%, the most likely single outcome. Scenario C: delayed or stalled, ~30%. Scenario D: external geopolitical or trade shock, ~15%. Scenario E: no project, and an alternative industrial policy counterfactual, ~10%.

Scenario B deserves particular attention because it is both the most likely and politically damaging. What gets built is a conventional advanced-electronics park with an ATP core, likely positive for the Philippines if its activity mix, utility costs and incentive terms hold up, and likely to be reported as a failure because the gap will be measured against 190,000 jobs and US$70bn. This is the strongest argument for the government to reset expectations now, before the numbers become the benchmark.

The outcome is most sensitive, in order, to: whether a named anchor reaches financial close with disclosed capital; whether firm power is delivered, when, and at what price; whether water storage is built and abstraction capped; whether the framework survives legal challenge; the global AI capex cycle; and US trade policy toward the Philippines. Three of the six turn on Philippine decisions by the executive, regulators and courts, and all three are currently unresolved. That is where policy effort should concentrate, because it is where effort changes outcomes.

[sources drawn on: T3-06 · T3-05 · T3-20]

### 22. Risk register
Twenty-one risks, with likelihood, impact, exposed parties and early-warning indicators.

The highest-likelihood risks are that investment does not materialise at announced scale; that job numbers are over-delivered on paper and under-delivered in fact; that fossil lock-in contradicts climate commitments; that terms are fixed at a disadvantage because the Year-3 rent and term remain undetermined at signature; that value capture remains thin in an enclave outcome; and that a good outcome is read as a failure.

The highest-impact risks are that water demand is met by reducing community or irrigation supply, an outcome that remains undetermined without a basin water balance; that a constitutional challenge under Article XVIII, Section 25 succeeds; and that concentrating strategic assets near Clark creates a physical targeting exposure.

One risk has already materialised. On 24 July 2026 the USTR imposed a 12.5% forced-labour tariff on Philippine exports, a deterioration in the economic relationship despite alignment. The Philippines was one of 60 economies investigated and has formed a response panel; its exports to the United States had grown 23.8% to US$6.68bn over January–May. The mitigation is to link framework concessions explicitly to trade-treatment commitments, and not to concede while penalties stand.

Two risks are worth naming because they are absent from official discussion. Corruption and rent-seeking in a large land-and-incentive programme is rated medium-high, against a record that includes 421 ghost projects among 8,000 inspected in flood control, and an unsolicited-proposal route already in use for the fuel pipeline. And data governance and IP leakage is rated medium-high, because no published provision addresses data localisation, lawful access, cross-border transfer, sovereign compute access or IP ownership for work done on Philippine soil. Across the register, the mitigations that recur are the same handful: milestone-based land release in tranches; performance-linked clawbacks; conditions precedent on firm power and financed water storage; published tax-expenditure estimates; NCIP engagement before signature; and a shorter initial term with performance-linked renewal rather than 99 years granted upfront.

[sources drawn on: T2-04 · T3-17 · T3-07 · T1-16 · T1-42]

### 23. Overall assessment
A serious strategic opportunity attached to a badly documented transaction.

The two things are separable, and almost all of the confusion in Philippine public debate comes from treating them as one. The strategic opportunity is real: an allied-supply-chain position that is genuine and time-limited, a credible upgrade path from back-end assembly into advanced packaging, and an urgent need for a growth engine as BPO faces AI displacement.

The transaction is badly documented. The operative instrument describes a coordination office, not an industrial district. Consideration is undetermined. The term is unstated. The map is missing. The studies behind every headline figure are unpublished. A published project-specific water balance was not located. DFC funding is for a gas feasibility study, not a committed generation plan; no final mix or off-site renewables-plus-firming design is established here. And no legal opinion has been published on whether the framework requires Senate concurrence.

None of that is an argument against the project. In fairness, some of the opposition is overstated too: the light-pollution claim exaggerates, the rare-earth-plunder claim is substantially overstated, and the dual-use critique in its strongest form proves too much, since dual-use characteristics are inherent to essentially all modern computing hardware. None of that is an argument against the project. All of it is an argument against signing on this record. No completion-time or negligible-cost guarantee is established for the independent studies, legal opinions and NCIP process. A strictly non-binding framework remains subject to the express safeguards in the two-branch rule.

[sources drawn on: T1-05 · T1-14 · T1-35 · T1-36 · T1-42]

### 24. Recommendations for the Philippine government
Thirty-nine recommendations, starting with eleven no-regret actions, most of them low-cost.

The immediate no-regret actions are largely within the executive’s control and would improve the Philippines’ position whether or not the project proceeds: publish Annex A; publish the draft framework with a comment period; correct the miscited charter; publish the underlying studies or withdraw the figures; impose single-source discipline on official statements; obtain and publish DFA-OLA and OSG opinions; formally engage the NCIP; commission independent water and grid studies; require NGCP to state its interconnection and reserve-margin position and the ERC to say who bears the cost of transmission reinforcement, the DOE having answered on 27 July; publish a tax-expenditure estimate; and require a written response to the Capas Local Government Code letter, publish the August consultation’s records and obtain Sanggunian resolutions, including Concepcion alongside Capas, Bamban and the province. Convening already occurred; formal follow-through remains the task.

Before any contract or construction: set the Year-3 rate and term against an independent valuation; resolve the exclusive-use clause; write an express Philippine governing-law and jurisdiction clause; make land handover conditional on financed firm generation and financed water storage, which is now the Energy Secretary’s stated position and not only this report’s recommendation, and record in the framework a defined on-grid ceiling consistent with the DOE’s 100–200 MW figure, with any load above it contingent on commissioned dedicated generation; require a project-specific ECC with a cumulative impact assessment; release land in tranches against verified capital and employment with automatic reversion of undeveloped tranches; write hard water conditions into the instrument; and add a data governance and IP annex including an allocation of sovereign compute for Philippine public and research use.

On medium-term industrial policy: attack the electricity cost gap directly, which is the single highest-return action available and is not contingent on Pax Silica; use minerals leverage instead of land concessions; target advanced packaging rather than fabs; fund supplier development and workforce programmes against the 128,000-worker goal; guarantee competitive neutrality through the PCC; and diversify anchors deliberately, because a zone with one anchor has the Intel-in-Cavite risk profile.

And on contingency: automatic reversion and clawback if milestones are missed; break clauses on defined non-performance; a shorter initial term of 25 years with performance-linked renewal; tenure-linked incentive recapture so a departing anchor repays what it consumed; and a published fallback plan for the 1,618.74 hectares if the project does not proceed.

[sources drawn on: T1-05 · T2-05]

### 25. Preconditions, safeguards and negotiating red lines
Seven preconditions before any rights-creating signature, eleven red lines that should not move, and a two-branch decision rule for November.

All seven preconditions must be met: the parcel legally defined and Annex A published; the draft framework published with a public comment period; independent water balance and grid adequacy studies published; the Year-3 rent and lease term determined against an independent valuation; DFA-OLA and OSG legal opinions published; the NCIP certification precondition process formally initiated; and the activity mix and all underlying economic studies published including the tax-expenditure estimate. If any is unmet, do not sign an instrument creating substantive rights. A strictly non-binding framework may be signed only with every express safeguard in the two-branch rule below; there is no established guarantee that all studies and statutory processes can finish within months.

The red lines: no application of foreign law to Philippine territory, and no immunity beyond general law; no restriction on Philippine regulatory jurisdiction inside the Zone; no stabilisation clause freezing environmental or labour standards; no exclusive-use grant to a foreign government at this scale without Senate concurrence; no lease with consideration left undetermined at signature; no 99-year term granted upfront without performance-linked staging; no commitment on mineral supply without a binding domestic processing obligation; no waiver of liability for contamination or worker injury; no classified annex withheld from the Senate; no transfer, sublease or collateralisation of the master lease without government consent on each occasion.

And one that is not a legal term at all: do not sign to meet another country’s summit calendar. If the terms are not ready in November, they are not ready in November.

These resolve into a two-branch decision rule, because the real red line is not the November ceremony but the creation of substantive rights before due diligence is complete. Branch one covers any binding instrument: do not sign anything that grants land possession or exclusive use, fixes a long lease term, leaves rent undetermined, restricts Philippine jurisdiction or regulatory authority, grants immunity, commits public infrastructure or fiscal incentives, creates mineral-supply obligations, permits subleasing, transfer or collateralisation of a land right, or gives any investor or foreign government preferred rights, unless all seven preconditions are satisfied first and the red lines are respected in the text. Branch two covers a strictly non-binding framework, which is acceptable and may even be tactically useful for the November milestone, but only if the text itself expressly states that it creates no lease or land right, confers no investor entitlement or exclusivity, commits no public funding or incentives, leaves every project subject to ordinary Philippine law and permits, allows either government to withdraw, and subjects every subsequent binding instrument to separate approval and public disclosure. A framework silent on those points should be treated as branch one.

So the question to ask of whatever is tabled in November is not "is it binding?" as a label. Under EO 459’s substance-over-nomenclature principle it is: what rights does this text create, and for whom? If the answer is "none, expressly," the signature is legally a photograph, although political lock-in may still follow. If the answer is anything else, the seven preconditions apply in full.

[sources drawn on: T1-05 · A-03]

### 26. Questions that must be answered publicly
Thirty-three questions to BCDA, the executive, the regulators, the United States and the investors.

To BCDA, the questions begin with the map and end with the open-space covenant, and include reconciliation of the disclosed payroll-withholding figure with wages and jobs, and the remaining components of total revenue, the employment multiplier behind 500,000–800,000 indirect jobs, the assumed domestic value-added share of US$200bn in exports, the identity of the "US-based company serving as project proponent," and, now answered on the recording, what was meant by wanting contracts "immune from any environmental situation."

To the executive, DFA and DOF: whether the framework goes to the Senate and on what legal opinion; what governing law and dispute forum will apply; whether a national security assessment has been conducted; what trade-treatment commitments the Philippines is seeking given the 12.5% tariff; and which body of government has formally approved the Philippine position, and when.

To the regulators: whether NCIP has initiated a certification precondition process and what the status of the Aeta CADT applications is; whether any project-specific ECC exists; on what technical analysis the NWRB sufficiency statement was made; how DOE and NGCP will serve 3 GW and who bears the reserve-margin risk; and whether the PCC will review the incentive package for competitive neutrality.

To the United States: what legal arrangements it considers necessary to operationalise the Zone, the question the State Department declined to answer in May 2026; what "joint governance" means concretely; what financial commitment exists beyond feasibility studies; whether it will accept an express dual-use exclusion clause; and how it reconciles designating the Philippines as the site of its flagship Zone with imposing a forced-labour tariff on Philippine exports. And to Foxconn specifically: given Wisconsin, will it accept performance-linked clawbacks tied to verified investment and hiring?

[sources drawn on: A-01 · A-04 · A-05 · A-06 · A-07 · A-08 · T1-35 · T1-36]

### 27. Indicators to monitor
What resolves within one year, three years and five years.

Within one year, the decisive period, watch whether a framework is signed in November and whether its text is published; whether Annex A, the water balance and the grid study appear; whether the Year-3 rent and term are fixed at signature, which is the clearest available signal of whether the Philippines negotiated or capitulated; whether the framework contains clawbacks, employment covenants and local-content obligations; whether the Senate asserts a concurrence role; whether any investor is named with a binding commitment and financial close; and whether Foxconn proceeds beyond due diligence, which is the single most informative signal available.

Within three years: actual capital deployed against the US$10bn initial target; whether site development began in Q1 2028; contracted and commissioned firm generation and water storage, ahead of load or behind it; verified employment against milestones and the foreign-worker share against the stated under-10%; realised tax revenue and published tax expenditure; and resolution or continued non-resolution of the Aeta CADT applications.

Within five years: the domestic value-added share of Zone exports, which is the single most important development metric; the number, revenue and employment of Philippine-owned supplier firms serving the Zone; whether any activity has moved beyond ATP into advanced packaging, design or materials; whether the industrial electricity price gap with Indonesia and Vietnam closed; water availability for Tarlac agriculture and drought performance; the compliance record; and whether the project’s emissions are consistent with the Philippines’ NDC.

[sources drawn on: T3-06 · T3-03 · T1-17]

### 28. Research limitations and evidence that could change the conclusions
What would move each judgment, and in which direction.

Publication of Annex A would establish the parcel needed to investigate the affected-household, catchment and CADT-overlap questions; resolving them also requires a mapped social baseline, water balance and relevant title/application records. It is the single highest-value disclosure available.

Publication of the underlying economic studies would either substantiate the headline figures or confirm that they are unsupported. A published activity mix would make every impact estimate falsifiable for the first time.

A signed, disclosed anchor lease with financial close would move the assessment materially toward Scenario A or B and away from C. Conversely, no anchor with financial close by Q2 2027 would move it toward C.

A published water balance showing a financed, permitted storage solution with a hard abstraction cap would substantially reduce the highest-impact risk in the register. A published energy plan reconciling the LNG feasibility study with the renewables framing would resolve the most clearly misleading item in the claim matrix.

[sources drawn on: A-01 · A-04 · A-05 · A-06 · T1-42]

### 29. Appendices
Documents register, calculation reference, discrepancy register, verbatim provisions, sources by tier, glossary, and prioritised information gaps.

Appendix A registers the key documents, distinguishing the publicly available, the Declaration, the US media note and fact sheet, the BCDA letter and Note Verbale, from those that are referenced but absent, chiefly Annex A, the Supplemental Agreement and the framework draft.

Appendix B sets out every calculation with its inputs and assumptions, at PHP 61.85 per US$1: the catchment formula, the storage requirement, the solar land requirement at the ACWA benchmark, the lease income present value, the withholding-tax reconciliation, and the export ratios.

Appendix C is a figure discrepancy register, a single table of every materially inconsistent number encountered, for use by anyone auditing official statements. Appendix D reproduces the operative provisions of the BCDA letter verbatim, since the wording has been widely paraphrased. Appendix E lists sources by evidence tier. Appendix F is a glossary. Appendix G prioritises the open information gaps by decisiveness.

[sources drawn on: T1-05 · T1-17 · T1-19 · T1-20 · T1-42]

## The decision frame (node, or not)

node, or not
What matters is whether the terms on the table in November beat the alternative. Both columns below are real; neither is costless.
path one
as a pax silica node
what the philippines gains
A named position inside an allied supply chain while comparative non-entanglement with Chinese capital is still a credible, time-limited asset.
A credible upgrade path from back-end assembly into advanced packaging, where industry value is migrating as transistor scaling slows.
An alternative growth engine as BPO, at 7.4% of GDP, faces AI-driven displacement.
BCDA’s projected PHP 60bn of lease income over 25 years, plus the option value of first-mover designation in a network intended to span continents.
Access to allied capital, the Stanford Foundry School curriculum, and Luzon Economic Corridor infrastructure momentum.
what it carries or forgoes
1,618.74 hectares committed, possibly for 99 years, at a rent that is currently "to be discussed."
3 GW on a grid that ran a 373 MW deficit under red alert three months before this report.
65–90 MLD of what is, at that scale, watershed water, in a Type I climate with a pronounced dry season.
An unquantified tax expenditure under CREATE MORE, including a 100% additional deduction on power for a multi-gigawatt load.
A named role in a strategy whose own fact sheet states the objective of displacing rival supply chains, borne physically by the Philippines.
path two
outside pax silica
what the philippines gains
No 99-year commitment, no grid increment, no watershed claim, no geopolitical targeting exposure.
The same political attention and institutional bandwidth, and any public resources the zone would otherwise absorb, could go toward closing the ~50% industrial electricity cost gap with Indonesia and Vietnam, which would benefit every existing locator, not one zone; prospective private zone capital would not itself be redirected.
Freedom to lead with minerals leverage rather than land concessions, on the Indonesian model.
Supplier development and workforce programmes for an electronics base that already earns US$46bn a year.
what it carries or forgoes
Forgone lease income of BCDA’s projected PHP 60bn over 25 years, with a present value of about PHP 25.6bn.
Forgone option value on a strategic position, and reputational cost with Washington.
The allied-advantage window is time-limited and closes without being used.
The manufacturing gap keeps widening while Malaysia moves into semiconductors, Thailand into automotive and Indonesia into nickel processing.
the assessment's own position
Neither endorsement nor rejection. The Philippines should decline to sign an instrument creating substantive rights before the seven conditions are met; a strictly non-binding framework is acceptable only with every express safeguard in the two-branch rule. Its legal leverage continues until substantive rights are created, though the November target can increase political pressure: it holds the asset, it has not yet signed, and the counterparty wants a deliverable for a presidential visit tied to the 80th anniversary of bilateral relations. A deadline set by another country's summit calendar is the worst possible reason to accept undetermined terms.

## Questions that must be answered publicly

questions that must be answered
Thirty-three questions, addressed to the parties who hold the answers. Most ask only for disclosure of work officials say they already hold; where that work does not exist, the answer is to say so and withdraw the figures it supported.
to BCDA
Where exactly is the parcel? Publish Annex A.
Does the exclusive-use clause at §II.3 permit private industrial locators such as Foxconn? If not, what instrument changes it, and under what authority?
Why does §III cite Republic Act No. 7277, the Magna Carta for Disabled Persons, as the Bases Conversion and Development Act, and why has it not been corrected?
What is the intended activity mix, in hectares and in capital?
Publish the studies behind every headline figure. Who conducted them, when, and on what assumptions?
How does the disclosed workers’ payroll-withholding projection reconcile with the employment and wage assumptions, and what comprises the rest of the PHP 180bn total?
What employment multiplier produces 500,000–800,000 indirect jobs, and from what source?
What is the assumed domestic value-added share of the US$200bn in exports?
What is the proposed lease term and Year-3 rate, and on what independent valuation?
Is the United States the master lessee? May it sublease, transfer or collateralise, and to whom?
Who is the "US-based company serving as project proponent," and how was it selected?
Publish the water balance, the impounding dam design and footprint, and the abstraction volumes sought.
Publish the energy plan, including the DFC-scoped 1,200 MW LNG plant, and reconcile it with the statement that the project aims to avoid fossil fuels.
What was meant by wanting contracts "immune from any environmental situation"?
What is the estimated cost of fiscal incentives and of public enabling infrastructure?
Is the 40% open-space commitment binding on this parcel, and how is it reconciled with maximal rainwater capture?
to the executive, DFA and DOF
Will the framework be submitted to the Senate? If not, on the basis of what legal opinion?
What governing law and dispute forum will apply?
Has a national security assessment of concentrating strategic assets at this site been conducted, and will it be published?
Given the USTR’s 12.5% tariff, what trade-treatment commitments is the Philippines seeking in return for the Zone?
Which body, Cabinet, NEDA Board, or otherwise, has formally approved the Philippine position, and when?
to NCIP, DENR, NWRB, DOE, NGCP and PCC
NCIP: has a certification precondition process been initiated? What is the status of the Aeta CADT applications over Capas filed in 1999, 2014 and 2019?
DENR: does any project-specific ECC exist for this parcel? Will a cumulative impact assessment be required?
NWRB: on what technical analysis was the sufficiency statement of 22 July 2026 made? Publish it.
DOE and NGCP: how will up to 3 GW be served, by when, at what cost, and who bears the reserve-margin and price risk?
PCC: will the incentive package be reviewed for competitive neutrality against existing PEZA locators?
to the United States
What legal arrangements does the United States consider necessary to operationalise the Zone, the question the State Department declined to answer in May 2026?
What does "joint governance" mean concretely, and what does "fuse American expertise in institutions and legal regimes" require of Philippine law?
What, if any, binding US financial commitment to implement the proposed zone exists beyond study-stage support? The separate signed MCC energy threshold grant is not identified as zone financing, and its terms remain unreviewed.
Will the Zone have any defence, dual-use or export-control function, and will the United States accept an express exclusion clause?
How does the United States reconcile designating the Philippines as the site of its flagship Economic Security Zone with imposing a 12.5% forced-labour tariff on Philippine exports?
to prospective investors, including Foxconn
Will you disclose your identity, capital commitment, employment commitment with a wage floor, technology-transfer commitment and local-content commitment as a condition of entry?
Foxconn specifically: given the Wisconsin experience, will you accept performance-linked clawbacks tied to verified investment and hiring?

## Claim checker (54 claims)

- [VERIFIED] (scope) Project area is 4,000 acres (1,618.74 ha) — claimed by US State Dept · BCDA. Verified as a stated figure. 4,000 ac × 0.404686 = 1,618.74 ha.
- [PARTIAL] (scope) Area equals 1,600 / 1,618 / 1,619 / 1,620 ha — claimed by Various. All are roundings of one US-stated acreage, not an independent Philippine survey.
- [FALSE] (scope) The parcel boundaries are defined — claimed by no claimant, assessed finding. The BCDA letter says boundaries "shall be determined by mutual agreement... set forth in a Supplemental Agreement". Annex A maps are referenced and absent from the published PDF. No mutually agreed parcel definition was located in the published instrument; this is a public-record finding, not proof that no internal map exists.
- [FALSE] (scope) The site is at the former Clark Air Base, Pampanga — claimed by Local and international outlets. New Clark City is in Capas and Bamban, Tarlac. A recurring media error.
- [UNKNOWN] (scope) "First AI-native industrial acceleration hub" — claimed by US State Dept · Helberg. An official designation with undefined content. Neither government has published a technical definition of "AI-native".
- [PARTIAL] (scope) No AI data centres will be located at New Clark City — claimed by DTI-BOI (Usec. Rodolfo) · BCDA. Verified as a repeated official statement, not as a land-use fact. Rodolfo told the House appropriations committee on 24 August 2026 "what’s clear is, in Clark, there is no data center", and that data centres "may happen in another location". But BCDA’s president said on 7 August that locators’ own-use data centres may be established "if ever", with only major ones outside the site; and BCDA’s own July 2025 bidder information lists a 47.0-hectare "Hyperscale Data Center" among New Clark City’s industrial locators. No instrument located sets the line between a permissible own-use facility and an excluded major one. On 1 September 2026 Palace Press Officer Claire Castro, attributing the position to the DTI, said "On the Clark Advanced Manufacturing Park, there will be no data centers" and that no proposal yet exists for another location outside New Clark City: the most categorical official assurance yet, and still not an instrument.
- [VERIFIED] (scope) The site is 17.1% of New Clark City — claimed by Derived. 1,618.74 ÷ 9,450 ha. Verified arithmetic.
- [PROJECTION] (money) US$40–70bn of investment at full development — claimed by BCDA (Bingcang). "Based on scientific studies, not speculation." The studies are unpublished and no investor is bound.
- [PROJECTION] (money) Initial investment requirement of US$10bn — claimed by BCDA. Funding source unstated, public, private, or which party.
- [VERIFIED] (money) Around 30 firms have expressed interest — claimed by BCDA. Verified as a statement of interest, not of commitment. None is named; BCDA says "we cannot entertain them yet fully".
- [UNVERIFIED] (money) 50+ firms including "trillion-dollar tech giants" — claimed by Reported. Inconsistent with BCDA's own figure of around 30.
- [PROJECTION] (money) Foxconn will anchor the hub — claimed by Finance Sec. Frederick Go. A named prospect, not a commitment. Go: "if Foxconn proceeds"; nothing is signed.
- [PROJECTION] (jobs) Foxconn would invest billions and generate "thousands of jobs" — claimed by Finance Sec. Go. The anchor’s unquantified “thousands” is far below the aggregate employment claim; no exact anchor headcount establishes a precise order-of-magnitude gap.
- [VERIFIED] (scope) The project is still at the planning stage and it is premature to release official information — claimed by BCDA. BCDA’s own words, refusing a Freedom of Information request for the project pipeline on 12 May 2026 under the pre-decisional and premature-disclosure exceptions. A second denial on 10 June 2026 withheld the site map. Tier-1 confirmation, by the proponent, that the project is pre-decisional and that the Annex A vacuum is deliberate.
- [FALSE] (money) A binding investment commitment exists — claimed by no claimant, assessed finding. None found as at the latest verification. BCDA states the framework must be finalised first.
- [UNVERIFIED] (money) AWS is discussing a US$5bn regional investment — claimed by Reported. Not corroborated; regional, not site-specific.
- [PROJECTION] (jobs) Over 130,000 high-quality jobs — claimed by BCDA. Official projection, 22 Jul 2026.
- [PROJECTION] (jobs) 130,000–190,000 direct and 500,000–800,000 indirect jobs — claimed by BCDA (Bingcang). Pairing low indirect with low direct employment and high with high gives an indirect-to-direct ratio of 3.8×–4.2×, not a total-employment multiplier or all possible endpoint combinations. The underlying model and pairing assumptions are unpublished.
- [PROJECTION] (jobs) "Nearly one million jobs" — claimed by Labor Sec. Francis Tolentino. Basis given as a comparison to "Taiwan’s industrial growth model". No labour standards, wage scales or training commitments stated.
- [PROJECTION] (jobs) Up to 300,000 jobs "as early as 2027" — claimed by Amb. Jose Manuel Romualdez. Timeframe irreconcilable with BCDA's own Q1 2028 construction start.
- [UNVERIFIED] (jobs) "Endless jobs" — claimed by US Amb. Lee Lipton. Stakeholder claim.
- [PROJECTION] (fiscal) PHP 180bn/yr in total government income at full operation — claimed by BCDA. Composition unpublished.
- [MISLEADING] (fiscal) PHP 68–75bn/yr in withholding tax — claimed by BCDA. BCDA specified the composition at the Palace briefing of 23 July 2026: tax contributed by the workers, i.e. payroll withholding. That forecloses the non-payroll explanation. At an assumed 20% effective rate and 160,000 workers, it implies average worker compensation of about PHP 2.13m, 2.4× a Philippine semiconductor engineer (PHP 870,938) and 8.1× an operator (PHP 263,118). As published, the tax and employment figures are therefore not reconciled at current wage benchmarks; which figure or assumption fails, only the unpublished model can say.
- [PROJECTION] (fiscal) PHP 60bn in lease income over 25 years — claimed by BCDA. Equals PHP 148.26/m²/yr. Present value at 8% real is about PHP 25.6bn, or 0.59%–1.03% of the projected investment. No independent land valuation has been published.
- [PROJECTION] (fiscal) US$200bn of exports associated with full build-out — claimed by BCDA. CORRECTION, 10 Aug 2026 — earlier versions described this as annual. New reporting places full development on an approximately 30-year horizon but does not consistently establish whether the figure is annual, cumulative over that horizon, or measured on another basis. The 2.37× comparison with the Philippines' US$84.48bn of 2025 merchandise exports is therefore a non-period-equivalent comparison of nominal magnitudes, not like-for-like annual flows.
- [PROJECTION] (fiscal) "About 10% of GDP" — claimed by BCDA. The domestic value-added assumption reconciling this with US$200bn of gross exports is unpublished, and it is the single most important number in any value-chain argument. Philippine electronics has historically captured a modest slice of gross flows because it imports most inputs and performs a narrow part of the process. JC Punongbayan of the UP School of Economics warns of exactly that outcome: the Philippines supplying "the land, minerals, power, water, and low-cost labor" while technology, patents, profits and strategic control remain abroad.
- [UNKNOWN] (fiscal) The cost of the fiscal incentive package — claimed by no claimant, assessed finding. No published estimate. CREATE MORE provides 5% SCIT or 20% CIT with enhanced deductions including a 100% additional deduction on power expenses, for up to 17–27 years. A material omission.
- [PROJECTION] (water & power) Water demand 65–90 MLD; design capacity 120 MLD, expandable to as much as 300 MLD — claimed by BCDA. Technically unsubstantiated. No water balance has been published. The 300 MLD expansion path, described at the 23 July Palace briefing, scales the required catchment to roughly 4,900–10,400 hectares, which is three to six times the entire parcel.
- [MISLEADING] (water & power) Water comes from rainwater harvesting, not community supply — claimed by BCDA. The required catchment is 90–193% of the site, so at 90 MLD this is watershed water rather than site water. Stated precisely: the on-parcel framing fails at the upper end of BCDA’s own demand estimate; what the appropriation does to downstream users is undetermined pending a catchment-level water balance, and the burden of proof sits with the proponent.
- [UNVERIFIED] (water & power) Water within the project area is sufficient — claimed by NWRB Exec. Dir. Sevilla D. David Jr.. No technical data, model or independent verification published.
- [MISLEADING] (water & power) The 60 million litres a day should not alarm the public: it equals one second of the combined discharge of all Zambales rivers, “only 60,000 cubic meters, which is one Panamax” — claimed by Rep. Jose “Pepito” Alvarez, vice chair, House appropriations committee. Said at the environment department’s 2027 budget briefing on 26 August 2026 — the first defence of the water requirement from the legislature. The unit conversion is right: 60 million litres is 60,000 cubic metres. Nothing else about the comparison is. It sets a daily demand against an instantaneous flow; a combined discharge of 60,000 cubic metres every second is an order no Philippine river system approaches, and no hydrological data was offered to the hearing or published after it; and it invokes the wrong catchment, since New Clark City sits in Capas, Tarlac and drains the Sacobia–Bamban system, not the western-draining rivers of Zambales. “Panamax” is a class of ship, not a unit of volume. The 60 million litre figure is also below BCDA’s own published range of 65 to 90 million. Kabataan Representative Renee Co replied at the same hearing that the concerns are not confined to water but extend to power and land. None of this changes the catchment arithmetic on this page.
- [PROJECTION] (water & power) Energy demand of about 3 GW at full development — claimed by BCDA. Independent technical commentary cites 5+ GW. Against the DOE’s official projection of 15,600 MW for 2026 Luzon peak demand, 3 GW is 19.2%; against the 14,534 MW actually recorded by mid-2026, it is 20.6%.
- [MISLEADING] (water & power) Power will be renewable; the project aims to avoid fossil fuels — claimed by BCDA. The US DFC is funding a feasibility study for a ≥1,200 MW LNG terminal and plant at the site. Solar equivalent to 3 GW would need about 15,000 ha, which is 9.3× the parcel.
- [MISLEADING] (water & power) The project "will not cut into current power supplies in the area" — claimed by BCDA. Supporting the assurance requires phase-specific supply, transmission and reserve adequacy before the actual load energises; full-build demand is not the initial phase, and nameplate capacity alone is not sufficient proof. BCDA’s president reiterated the assurance on 9 August 2026, saying proponents were studying a dedicated power plant; a study does not establish that capacity. Presented as unconditional.
- [PARTIAL] (water & power) 40% of the site is reserved as open or green space — claimed by BCDA · NCC master plan. Applies to the NCC master plan generally; not shown to bind the Pax Silica parcel, and incompatible with maximal rainwater capture.
- [PARTIAL] (environment) All investments require an Environmental Compliance Certificate — claimed by BCDA · DENR. Overstated as put. ECCs attach to Category A and B projects, not to all investments (DAO 2003-30 §§4.1, 4.4, 4.6; a Certificate of Non-Coverage covers Category D). Correction (v2.38): this note previously said the estate "unambiguously requires an ECC with a full EIS" and that "None is on the public record". Both are withdrawn. BCDA has published ECC-OL-R03-2019-0304 (24 Jun 2019), in which EMB classified the 9,450-hectare New Clark City Land Development Project under EMB MC 2014-005 item 3.6.5 — "Industrial Parks (horizontal development) with critical slopes", requiring an EIS at 5 hectares and above — and issued an ECC after an EIS was submitted. What survives: the certificate enumerates no manufacturing, semiconductor, data-centre or mineral-processing component; its Restriction 25 subjects any expansion or modification of approved components to new EIA requirements and requires individual locator ECCs; DENR reported on 26 Aug 2026 that no Pax Silica-specific EIA application and no clear project description had reached the EMB; and no cumulative impact assessment was located in the reviewed record.
- [VERIFIED] (environment) There will be no mining inside the project area — claimed by BCDA. Verified as to extraction on site; incomplete as to consequences. The US fact sheet cites "enhanced access to the Philippines’... mineral endowments" and refining is a listed on-site activity.
- [MISLEADING] (environment) Pax Silica will drive rare-earth and nickel plunder — claimed by Kalikasan PNE · AGHAM · CPU · KMP. Substantially overstated as applied to semiconductors. Silicon is ~95% of semiconductor material demand and the Philippines is not a silicon producer; per-mineral end uses: nickel is ~65–70% stainless steel with batteries ~10–15% and rising; cobalt was 76% lithium-ion batteries in 2024, of which EVs ~43% and portable electronics ~30%, with stainless nil; chromite is ~90–96% metallurgical and ferrochrome, over 80% of that to stainless. Semiconductor demand for these minerals is negligible, confirmed against USGS, INSG, Cobalt Institute and ICDA breakdowns. A narrower minerals concern survives.
- [MISLEADING] (environment) Data centres will cause light pollution disrupting wildlife — claimed by Advocacy groups. Substantially overstated, but a legitimate and mitigable EIA screening item. Data centre interiors are essentially unlit; exterior lighting is not. 24/7 perimeter security, parking, roads and the construction phase are a documented ecological disruptor per US DOE Solid-State Lighting guidance and DarkSky International’s statement specifically on data-centre light pollution, and readily mitigated with full-cutoff fixtures, lamps at 3000K or below, and curfew dimming. Campaigners would be better served narrowing this point than dropping it.
- [UNVERIFIED] (legal & social) Clark Freeport exceeds 30,000 ha, of which 15,000+ ha are already allocated to indigenous groups — claimed by BCDA. Offered by BCDA in support of its no-displacement position. Not independently verified in this review, and it concerns the wider Clark Freeport rather than the Pax Silica parcel.
- [DISPUTED] (legal & social) No indigenous community will be displaced — claimed by BCDA · Malacañang. Turns on titled versus claimed domain. Aeta CADT applications over Capas were filed in 1999, 2014 and May 2019. Under IPRA, native title and FPIC obligations do not depend on a CADT having issued. Section 59 goes further: it bars any government agency or government-owned corporation from issuing a lease or concession without NCIP certification that the area is not overlapped, and its proviso covers pending applications, so a new BCDA lease would be barred outright if the parcel overlaps the Aeta claims filed in 1999, 2014 and 2019. At the Senate hearing of 14 August 2026, materially different population figures were put on the record: BCDA’s expressed in households, NCIP’s at 75 households, and about 1,000 people reported by a community witness as Sitio Sapang Kawayan’s own census. The hearing’s auto-generated transcript adds the provenance: NCIP told the committee it has no exact validated count and that the 75 came through an IP community source covering one sitio within the proposed area, while BCDA described about 14 houses seen on an earlier visit and speculated it might now be 30. A separate affected population also emerged — two preliminary farmer lists for a first phase of about 580 hectares, 182 associated with BCDA and 266 in the municipality’s own records, with financial assistance offered at ₱30 per square metre and no designated relocation site for that group. The first phase’s own extent is stated inconsistently: at a New Clark City briefing on 7 August 2026 BCDA president Joshua Bingcang described it as “around 500 hectares”. Both figures are approximate and the record does not establish whether they share a boundary, a scope or a reference date, and no published phase-boundary document was located — so the variation is recorded, not resolved, since the farmer counts are keyed to a phase extent. They are not directly comparable — two count households, one counts people, and the reporting does not establish that they cover the same area or the 1,618.74-hectare parcel — so none is a verified count. What the exchange does show is that no current, published, parcel-specific enumeration was located, which is also what a categorical assurance of no displacement would need. On-site reporting published 18 August 2026 adds the residents’ own account: Ralph Gelmar Lozano said he and other residents were told their houses would be affected and that they could be required to leave by December, and Antero Capiz separately recalled being told they had only until Christmas; residents said they had not been told where they would be relocated or what assistance would be provided, and that payment would cover their houses but apparently not the land. This is reported testimony, not an agency record — no BCDA notice, valuation schedule, relocation plan or demolition order corresponding to a December date has been published, and the reporting does not identify by name or institutional affiliation who communicated those dates. Correction (v2.32): this report previously read the clearest discrepancy as lying between BCDA’s lower household estimate and NCIP’s 75-household figure. That characterisation is withdrawn. The same 18 August ABS-CBN report attributes the approximately 1,000-person figure to chieftain Petronila Capiz-Munoz by name, and reports NCIP Chairperson Nancy Catamco saying the chieftain had initially reported 75 households or families — so the 75 may not be independent of the community evidence behind the 1,000. The attribution v2.26 withdrew is reintroduced solely as an ABS-CBN-reported claim, not from the hearing transcript; that earlier withdrawal remains accurately recorded as a correction made on the evidence then available. The report does not conclude the two community-associated figures are comparable: no common reference date, geographic scope, population definition or counting unit is established, and "households or families" is itself ambiguous. The NCIP announced on 20 August 2026 that it had conducted or begun a census and validation of Aeta Hungey households at Sitio Sapang Kawayan, reported by the Daily Tribune on 21 August and carried by Rappler, Brigada Balita, NET25 and News5, several expressly crediting that announcement; no household, family or person total from it has been identified, and nothing published identifies it as a Section 59 field-based investigation, a Certification Precondition process or an FPIC proceeding, nor places it outside them. On 4 September 2026 BCDA published its own account of the work for the first time — a press release describing an updated census at Sitio Sapang Kawayan led by NCIP Secretary Nancy A. Catamco and BCDA officer-in-charge senior vice president Mark P. Torres — and told reporters the same day that the exercise is “an update and validation of the existing community census, rather than a new enumeration” and that “we are still consolidating and validating the final figures with the NCIP, and we will provide the official numbers once the process is completed”. That is the proponent itself saying the numbers are not ready. No final official total resulting from the update was located as at 5 September 2026, and whether this is the same field exercise NCIP announced on 20 August, a continuation of it, or a related validation is not established. As at 5 September 2026 no current, published, parcel-specific enumeration reporting households and persons on a common reference date has been identified, and until one is, none of the reported figures can be treated as independently verified. This report elsewhere carries the GMA spelling Petroniza Capriz-Muñoz; both source-specific spellings are preserved and neither is resolved.
- [DISPUTED] (legal & social) Only about 10 farmers are affected — claimed by BCDA. Campaigners cite ~20,000 Aeta and farmers; historical NCC-wide figures cite 65,000 people in 12 villages including ~18,000 Aeta. Unresolvable without Annex A.
- [VERIFIED] (legal & social) A two-year rent-free grace period is offered — claimed by BCDA letter. The letter’s lease table lists "In-kind Contribution of the Philippines" as the Annual Lease Rate for the Lease Period "Years 1-2 (Grace Period)", and its text says: "The grace period of two (2) years on lease payments shall be considered as a tangible offer of in-kind contribution of the Philippines for the development of the two countries’ bilateral economic security." Worth roughly PHP 4.8bn at the rent implied by BCDA’s own figures.
- [UNKNOWN] (legal & social) The Year-3 lease rate — claimed by BCDA letter. Verified that it is undetermined. The published table reads "To be discussed."
- [UNKNOWN] (legal & social) The lease term — claimed by BCDA letter. No term is stated anywhere in the document. BCDA separately cites the 99-year ceiling under RA 12252.
- [PROJECTION] (fiscal) If a hub is built at New Clark City there is "no budget requirement from us" — "they will pay us rent", making it revenue-enhancing — claimed by DOF Secretary Frederick Go. The published instrument setting out the proposed land terms provides a two-year rent-free period and does not quantify the rent from Year 3 or state a lease term. The published record therefore does not establish the rent stream the characterisation depends on. "No budget requirement from us" appears to refer to cash budget requirements and does not account for the non-cash economic value of the two-year rent-free period, which the proposal identifies as the Philippines’ in-kind contribution.
- [PARTIAL] (legal & social) Investors may lease for up to 99 years under RA 12252 — claimed by BCDA. Verified as to the law, unverified as to this project, and narrower than the citation implies. The 99-year regime under RA 7652 as amended covers private lands leased by qualifying foreign investors with approved and registered investments. New Clark City land is held by BCDA, but its classification for purposes of RA 7652 and RA 12252 has not been established in the public record, which raises a threshold question about whether the regime applies at all; the statute alone does not establish authority for a master lease to a foreign-government entity.
- [DISPUTED] (legal & social) The US sought diplomatic immunity and US jurisdiction — claimed by BCDA (Bingcang). Helberg: "We never said our goal was to maintain diplomatic immunity... patently untrue." The State Department declined to answer the direct question on 26 May 2026.
- [DISPUTED] (legal & social) The project is purely commercial, with no defence function — claimed by Helberg · BCDA. Not sustainable as stated. Amb. Romualdez links Pax Silica revenue to the country becoming "more militarily equipped"; the US fact sheet frames the network as displacing rival supply chains. That is a strategic-security and revenue linkage, not evidence of an on-site military or defence-production function, which is not established. No dual-use exclusion clause is published.
- [VERIFIED] (scope) Pax Silica has 25 signatories — claimed by US State Dept. CORRECTION, 1 Aug 2026 — this site previously published "24 signatories" as verified. That was accurate when checked on 26 June 2026; Italy signed the Declaration at Brindisi on 31 July 2026 as the 25th signatory, and the count is now 25. Still widely miscounted as 13, 14, 15, 23 or "about 30". One signatory, the EU, is not a country. Saudi Arabia has been wrongly listed.
- [FALSE] (scope) "More than 30 countries" have joined Pax Silica — claimed by BCDA · Palace briefing, 23 Jul 2026. Stated twice to national media. The State Department count on that date was 24 signatories, unchanged since the Second Summit four weeks earlier, and one of the 24 is the EU rather than a country.
